speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a brief reference to a despatch from London of the 12th of May, which deals with a question which I apprehend will be one of great interest to Canadians, and refers to an abuse which I think ought to receive some notice from this House. The despatch is as follows ;
A court-martial is in progress at Dublin against certain officers of the 21st Lancers. They are accused of ' ragging ' a brother officer. Lieutenant Willows. Lord Roberts is in Dublin to-day and is especially interesting himself in the trial. Williams is a colonial ranker who gained his commission through heroism displayed in the South African war. He takes his profession seriously. His brother officers ragged him first because he had risen from the ranks, and secondly because he is a colonial. This kind of a scandal is common in many regiments where commissions are held by colonial rankers. The ordinary English officer considers the army a social preserve and not a public service.
With regard to this matter, we have from time to time accounts in the press of affairs of this nature. We have the fact revealed that among the aristocratic officers in the British army, there is not only prejudice against men risen from the ranks, but a double prejudice against men who have risen from the ranks and are colonials. This prejudice develops into violent action towards these officers. There are cases where they have been subjected to the most shameful indignities and violent treatment, and where such treatment has been visited upon them, not because they are not military officers worthy of the positions they hold, but because they do not belong to a certain grade of the aristocracy, because they are not patricians. We find that Britishers seem to have bowed to the circumstances and resigned themselves to this kind of usage without making much fuss about it, but I apprehend that colonials will hardly take this treatment with as much complacency. I do not think it is out of place to call attention in the House to this matter, and I desire to put on record my protest, as an individual member of parliament and a Canadian citizen, against the treatment meeted out to our fellow colonials in the imperial service. The best blood of the country, the most successful business men, the ablest public men, professional and military, have come from the middle classes. These classes have always outstripped those above and those below them, and surely no policy should be tolerated that discriminates against men who owe their promotion not to social influence, but to merit and bravery. I can conceive of no greater outrage to an officer like Lieutenant Willows, who owes his commission, not to social influences but to distinguished bravery in the British service in South Africa, than the 1 ragging ' to which he was subjected by the patricians of the 21st lancers. All history gives us

information and experience as to the value of the class of men who rise from the ranks The great marshals of Napoleon, the great soldiers, the men whose fame spread over the world, were men who came from the ranks because of their intrinsic qualities, because of their superior capacity, demonstrated in the field of practical experience, and that is the place to demonstrate whether a man possesses the qualities that will make him famous or not. These qualities are not due to the fact that he happens to belong to the aristocracy, that he happens to be the son of a duke, of an earl, or of a lord, but are brought out in the crucial test of active military duties. In the civil war, which made the United States a great military nation, the most famous names in that struggle, with the exception of a few West Pointers, were those of men who had risen from the ranks. And even these graduates of West Point were boys, selected from the middle class, recommended by their respective members of congress, and sent to that military academy, from which they graduated and entered the army. There is no other military service in the world, I venture to say, where the conditions in the respect I have mentioned, are such as exist in the British army. There is no other military service in which a man who receives a commission because of merit and bravery will not be accepted as a proper companion for those whose social standing is a little better than his own. The British army, in my opinion, should be made a fighting machine and not a social preserve. It should not be a place intended to afford positions to patricians, where they may lord it over those below them, but should be made a fighting machine composed of the best material obtainable, and if it were, the British army would be the best in the world. If anything would detract from this and render it less efficient, it is the kind of thing described in this despatch which I have just read. A few weeks ago, the death occurred of a ' ranker,' one of the bravest of the brave, a man who had acquired as enviable a military reputation as any man who ever belonged to the British army. I refer to the late General Sir Hector Macdonald. True there were charges made against him, but the charges were never tried and the law supposes him to be innocent until proved guilty. He had a brilliant military record, yet he was treated in a manner a little better than shameful, so far as the authorities were concerned. His treatment was due largely to the prejudices of the British aristocratic classes against men who have come from the ranks and who belonged to the middle classes and not to the patrician order. When we talk of imperial unity and hear arguments in favour of imperial defence, when we are asked to tax ourselves for that purpose, I would like to ask what influence will be exerted in favour of such a line of policy by the treatment given to Lieu-1 Mr. CHARLTON.
tenant Willows and, in numerous other instances, to colonials who have risen from the ranks ? If the British people expect Canada to fall in with their views on imperial unity and to aid in the defence of the British empire, they will have to see that in the army fair play be made the rule, that merit be recognized as it should be, and that colonists should have their sons, who have gained promotion in that army through their merits, placed on the same social grade, as the best men in the British army, so far as blood is concerned. Our people will resent this outrage perpetrated on an independent colonial citizen by imperial officers because forsooth he is not a patrician. I have a right to protest as an individual, and I do so in the hope that my protest may be heeded, because a perpetuation of this kind of treatment to which I have referred, will have an effect most lamentable, so far as the relations of the colonials and the motherland are concerned.

I did not know that my hon. friend intended bringing this matter up, or I perhaps would have been a little better prepared to say something with reference to the particular case to which he has referred. But I cannot help taking the view at the outset that my hon. friend has departed somewhat from the sound doctrine which he laid down in this House, not very long ago, namely, that we had perhaps enough to do in attending to our own business without interfering with that of the imperial parliament. It seems to me, if the exception which he took on that occasion was good, it would be very much stronger in the case which he has brought up to-day, which is purely a case of discipline within the British army itself, with which we can possibly have nothing to do. However, I may refer briefly to what my hon. friend has said. There is no doubt that in certain aristocratic regiments of the British army, there is a strong prejudice against what are called rankers, or men who rise from the ranks. I do not think, however, that that is at all general throughout the British army, nor do I believe that the prejudice is any stronger against the colonial ranker than any other. The hon. gentleman has intimated that Canadians have not received fair play in the British army. I do not think that that is a fair statement. Let us look at men in the British army, distinguished Canadians like Girouard who, in South Africa was placed in one of the most responsible positions in the army, being the right-hand man of the commander-in-chief for a long time during the concluding months of the war. I might mention many other Canadians, not only graduates of the Royal Military College, but men who have gone from the active militia of this country, and have been treated fairly in the British army, and from 1 whom no complaint whatever has been

heard. So, I think it is hardly fair to charge that there is a determination, a preconcerted determination, on the part of British officers or the British authorities to place Canadians who become officers of the British army at a disadvantage as compared with officers born in the British islands. I do not think that is the intention of the British authorities, and it seems to me only fair that I should make that statement here.

maintopic: SUFFERERS FROM FIRES IN THE OTTAWA VALLEY. '
SUFFERERS FROM FIRES IN THE OTTAWA VALLEY. '
speechtext:
(Translation.) I wish to call the attention of the government to the destruction caused by fires in the valley of the Ottawa, and more particularly in the county of Labelle. The poor settlers who have been burnt out are now deprived of all the necessaries of life for themselves and their families. All has been destroyed, their dwellings, their barns, their agricultural implements. I do not mention the minor losses sustained by several other people, through the destruction of hedges or of live stock in the pastures.
I think I am not mistaken in saying that the government granted relief to the sufferers of Russell county, a few years ago, when great fires devastated that region. It is also to my knowledge that we voted large sums for the relief of the sufferers in the great Hull and Ottawa fire. I hope the government will deem it as reasonable, in the present instance, to grant assistance to the sufferers from the fires in the valley of the Ottawa.
These unfortunate settlers are in a most lamentable position. They have lost all their property at the very time when they were the least capable of facing such a contingency. Most of them settled on these new lands not more than four or five years ago, at the cost of great sacrifices. They opened up roads, cleared their lands, built houses for themselves ; but as yet they have not reaped any benefit. As a matter of fact their position is almost a desperate one. If the public do not extend relief, many of them will have to abandon their farms. It is stated (and truly, I think), that a contented settler is the best colonization agent that could be found. It is, to my mind, equally true to say that a disheartened settler is the worst enemy of colonization. The public are, therefore, interested in relieving at once the really grievous condition in which these settlers are, not only with a tiew to helping these poor people out of the calamity which has befallen them, but also with a view to preventing the exit of settlers which Is threatening this region. To my mind it is the only means whereby settlers in these parts, after having sustained such great losses, may be induced to remain on their farms.
We are making constant sacrifices to promote and develop the settlement of the
North-west Territories. I do not object to that; but it seems to me it should not make us lose sight of the condition of the settlers in the older provinces. We are going to great expenditures with the object of attracting to our country immigrants from various European countries ; we are helping on foreign immigration. With still more reason should we endeavour to prevent our own people, those who have made sacrifices to open up new lands, from leaving the country, as this contingency would soon have its counterpart in another, just as sad, by discouraging those who would otherwise have been disposed to settle on, and clear, our new lands.
I trust, therefore, that the government will tender some assistance to the relief committees organized for the purpose of helping the sufferers from the fires in the Ottawa valley.
The PRIME MINISTER (The Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier(. (Translation.) speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say, for my own part, that I think

we should not pass over the matter Introduced by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) In such a way as to leave the impression outside of this House, and perhaps with the mother country, if the incident be noticed there at all, that this House, or the members of this House, or the Canadian people, look upon the system generally described as ' ragging ' with anything like favour. I think it is quite proper that the Minister of Militia (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) should have made the remarks he did, so as to guard this House, and, I presume the members of the House generally, from any imputation of charging misconduct generally against the officers of the British service, or any class In the British islands. As I understand it ' ragging ' is not a matter of regular discipline, but rather a system of punishment established by the mess or by the association in connection with the mess of a regiment, a sort of club constituted of the officers of the regiment, which undertakes to impose punishments for infraction of the arbitrary rules which it undertakes to enforce. And these punishments take an insulting and belittling form, as I have learned. Generally speaking, the great interest in this matter for us is the fact that there is a large-and likely to be larger-number of young and educated Canadians, very largely educated and trained at the expense of the Canadian people, who are passing into the British army, and taking their places there as commissioned officers. There is a provision, as I understand it, under which His Majesty gives a certain number of commissions regularly to the graduates of the college we maintain. So, I think, Canadians are interested in seeing to it that the men whom we send there, who, so far as mental ability, courage and professional qualifications are concerned, are we believe, at least the equals of the officers born in the British islands-we should see to it that these gentlemen are treated as gentlemen when they go into the British service ; and, if they are not so treated, we should give the impression to the people of the British islands that we have no sympathy with the system of absurdities and nonsense that interferes with proper military discipline. Therefore, I think it would be unfortunate to allow this matter to pass as though the people of Canada had any sympathy with such absurdities. From what I have seen in the press and heard in conversation with soldiers from South Africa, where our sons fought side to side with the British regulars and under British officers, I have gained the impression that, though our men have come back with a highly developed respect for ' Tommy Atkins,' on the other hand, many of them have formed the opinion that the British officer is not the man he ought to be, if the British army is to continue to be what it has been. The British private has courage, and all the qualities that have given us our extraor-Mr. BELL.
dinary military record. But, as I gather from the reports in the newspapers and from what I have been told by returned soldiers, too much is the officer given up to sport, too much is he attracted by social considerations, and too much is he influenced by the official rank. As citizens of Canada, and of what is unquestionably, next to the mother country, the greatest partner in the imperial federation which we hope to see accomplished, which we hope to see go on from one stage of accomplishment to another, we have a direct interest" in the efficiency of the British army ; and I think it is not out of place that we should, in a case of this kind, where a brother, a friend, a fellow countryman is affected, state that, so far as we are concerned, we look with great disfavour upon the system which is called ' ragging,' and are inclined to regard with a great deal of displeasure any instance in which its indignities are inflicted upon a Canadian.

maintopic: 'RAGGING' IN THE BRITISH ARMY.
speechtext:
It is not my intention to take up much of the time of the House in dealing with this subject. I had expected an utterance from the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) upon this subject. He gave us a lecture the other day which, I think, has not very much pleased either himself or the general public. I must say I heartily endorse the views expressed by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell). Now, ' ragging ' in the service, as I understand it, is as it has been defined by the hon. member for Pictou. But there is more than that, there is this social ostracism, there is forcing the men to follow certain lines and ways. I want to tell this House that this is not by any means a colonial complaint, it is a complaint on the part of the best men in the British service, sons of the highest noblemen who have entered the service with a desire of becoming proficient in their profession, so that in case they should fever be called upon to do duty for their country they would be as well posted and as efficient as possible. But the social etiquette- I think that term will include the entire cause of complaint-is such that it prevents a man from devoting his attention to the service; and as a consequence, men who have gone into the service with the highest ambition to be a credit to their country have left the army broken hearted. Their high spirit would not stand the humiliating mode of social life that these officers have unfortunately to lead. Of course we know that these officers as a rule have very little to do. The best men are either lost to the service entirely, or they have to fall in with the current custom which is in vogue in the army.
The Minister of Militia has referred to the Canadians who have risen in the service. I am glad, Sir. that Canadians have risen in the service, but it is chiefly in the engin-

eers. I want to point out that the custom of ragging cannot prevail in the engineers department because there is no regimental etiquette or mess among these. Those faults we find belong chiefly to the cavalry regiments. But we do not find in the engineer's' corps anything like the mess service or the regimental esprit de corps which you find in others. I shall not enter into a detailed discussion of that matter to-day, but I want to point out that the complaint does not come from colonials alone, but from the best men in the British service.
There is another matter of much importance to us colonials. We send our officers over there for training. I do not know whether we always pick our best men; I presume it is rather difficult to get a good man to settle down into a military life in a country like Canada. But whether we pick the best men or not, it is unfortunate that Canadian officers-and I wish the Minister of Militia to make a note of that and examine into it, I do not want him to take my word for it-but I say it is unfortunate that Canadian officers who have gone into training in the imperial service, or who are in our permanent corps, seem as a rule to adapt themselves to the objectionable features of the regular service, and do not become sufficiently posted on important matters of their duty. I want to say that the customs of the British service undoubtedly reflect upon ours. These improper customs are not peculiar to the British service. We find the tyranny of the German service infinitely greater than that of the British. Why, only the other day, the press of the conn try was filled with a story where a young German officer meeting a non-commissioned officer and not considering himself properly saluted, shot the non-commissioned officer, and he has been upheld by the German Emperor himself, I understand. Why, Sir, any such condition of affairs in the British dominions would bring on a revolution inside of an hour, and rightly so. If the King of England even endorsed any such attitude on the part of the officers, there would be a republic proclaimed throughout the British dominions before twenty-four hours were over.

speechtext:
I am afraid I would not be able to cover my hon. friend. My proportions are not sufficiently broad a shelter to my hon. friend, either in advance or in retreat. Reference has been made to South Africa. It is a well-known fact-and I have shown, and I trust will show again, that I appreciate the British army as highly as any man should appreciate an army-but I want to point out this fact, that when Canadians went to South Africa, when colonials of all sorts went to South Africa, while Canadians did splendid service there, and while the Canadian soldier, I think, was the best man in Africa, still I must say 99
that the Australian and the New Zealander, officer and man, was considered ahead of him, taking them altogether. I had a very good opportunity of knowing that the New Zealand officer and the Australian officer was better individually than the Canadian officer, taking them man for man. But the point I wish to make is this, that when the colonials went to South Africa it was never the intention that they should see fighting- we might as well understand that. It was a very short time before the colonials were raised and sent to South Africa, that the highest officers in the British service in the colonies, informed the Prime Minister of Canada and informed the British government that colonials in the imperial service would be a ' menace ' to their armies in South Africa, that is the word, would be a ' menace ' to British arms in South Africa. When the cojonials reached South Africa they were regarded with considerable curiosity, looked at through various eye-glasses, and regarded as rather fit subjects to guard lines of communication, to be posted along wayside stations and that sort of business. The idea was utterly abhorrent to the imperial officers that these men could possibly take their places in the field in the line of battle alongside the British troops. I want to point out that it was not until after the memorable engagements of Stormberg, Ma-gersfontein and Colenso, that colonial troops began to be recognized. It was not until after the strategy and tactics of the British officers had been proven to be absolutely at fault, when the whole British army in South Africa stood face to face with the most deplorable position that it has ever been in, it was only then and not till then that one solitary Canadian, one solitary Australian or New Zealander, was ever put into the fighting line.
However, I do not know that this is pertinent to the subject of ragging. I have very little respect for the colonial who would waste his time, a man who has arrived at mature years, who would waste his time, being a regular officer under existing conditions. I may say, and I say it frankly, that I have a son whom, in former days, it was my highest ambition to see in the field wearing the uniform of a British officer. But after my experience-I do not think I would be justified in saying that I would prefer to follow my son to the grave-but I will say that I would as soon see him in any other position as following the profession of a British officer. I am glad to say that he refused a position in the imperial army, one of the highest positions given to Canadians, the Royal Engineers in India; he refused the commision of his own accord. Had he asked my advice in the matter, I would have told him frankly to refuse it. As to the matter of preventing ragging, it is a matter of turning the whole life of the British officer inside out, it is a matter of giving to the middle class in Britain, men who have only their own



honour and the honour of their country to uphold, giving them an opportunity to come to the front. To-day it is an open boast in Britain that since the days of commission-purchasing, other systems have arisen which make it just as impossible for a man coming from the middle classes in Britain to rise from the ranks to get a commission in the army or to obtain prominence in it, as it was before. They openly boast that the aristocracy of England will control the officers. With that I have no fault to find, but this condition must be established that the officer shall be trained as highly, shall be a gentleman in his demeanour and as proficient a soldier as it is possible for him to be. It will not do for him to be a Piccadilly dude ; he must make himself efficient, and if ever a colonial or man from the middle ranks in England should be granted a commission, such a person must be accorded the same rights as he himself enjoys. Otherwise, as far as the view's of the great majority of people in Britain, as well as those of the colonies are concerned, the whole system of officers' promotion and training will have to be changed and a purely promotion system will have to be instituted. I may tell the House that I know that already magnificent reforms have been made in the army system by the people of Britain. A few already have been introduced into the cavalry corps which has been referred to by the hon. member for North Norfolk, since the close of the war, and I know that it is the determination of the British people and government. notwithstanding the Gibraltar of opposition. to rid the army entirely of the barnacles that have so. long prevented its progress towards the perfection to which the British army officer should attain. I want to say here that there are thousands of the best officers in the service who will welcome with open arms the change such as has been outlined by the hon. member for North Norfolk, any change that will give them an opportunity of standing on their merits, of being able to make themselves proficient and letting them win their positions by merit and not by society influence. There is no class that I can call to mind at the present moment that will welcome a change like that more cordially than the great majority of British officers in the service to-day. I know this to be a fact. These officers have pointed out again and again the futility of their attempting to make themselves proficient under the present system. If the lion. Minister of Militia and Defence introduces his Bill into this House in relation to the service, I trust he will take note of the fact that there shall be no star-chamber reports by one officer concerning another, that no reports shall ever be made by a superior officer concerning another officer, but which the officer concerned will first see and will show' that he has seen it by endorsing his name tliere-Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
on. That is one of the great drawbacks in the imperial service to-day. More than that we should insist that the system of training shall be such that merit will count on every occasion. However, these matters are coming mi at a later period of the session, and I shall not detain the House further on the present occasion.

maintopic: INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to bring to the attention of the House, and particularly to the attention of the government, a matter that is creating a great deal of adverse criticism in the press of the province of Manitoba at the present time, and which is, in fact, becoming a public scandal owing to the extent to which it has taken place. I refer to the participation of Dominion civil servants in the elections about to take place in the province of Manitoba. I do not desire to go particularly into the question of dismissals, which has been very thoroughly threshed out in preceding sessions, but I merely desire to bring to the attention of the government the law that was laid down in I89(i when these discussions were up, by which the government intended to guide their future actions in reference to officials participating in active political warfare, and I will give some specific instances where that law has been grossly violated, which. I think, demand the immediate attention and action of the government.' It has been laid down as a cardinal principle by the members of the cabinet, particularly in their speeches of 1890, that a person cannot be at tlie same time a civil servant and a political partisan, that he must do either one of two things-he must either cease to be an active partisan or cease to be a civil servant. Dismissals innumerable have taken place since this government have come into power, of officials whose political proclivities were Conservative, on the ground that they were active participants in political warfare, that they had served as active members of political committees, that they had been seen on political platforms, that they had participated in election discussions, that they had canvassed from house to house and that in other respects they were actively engaged in political warfare in the interest of the candidates of the party to which they belonged. Many of these dismissals have taken place without any investigation having been held, without allowing them any chance to defend themselves. Many of them have taken place upon 1he mere request of the Liberal representative in parliament, or of the defeated Liberal candidate, or of some political committee to whom had been entrusted the duty of demanding the head of the accused person. Now. Sir, with this established as a precedent on the part of the government, and particularly when we review the speeches of the hon. gentlemen during the session of 1890. and when we have no attempt to justify this action on their part, I think that with the instances I will lay before the government to-day, we may fairly claim that the government should be called upon to immediately put into execution this principle to which they gave 99*
their adherence and at once dismiss these officials who have violated the law as laid down by themselves. In the first place, I desire to refer to some remarks of the right hon. leader of the government when this question of dismissals was up during the session of 1896, and an expression by the bight hon. gentleman should have far more importance attached to it because of the position which he occupies, than of any other hon. member of the House, or than of any other member of the cabinet. I may say that I largely agree with the views laid down by the Prime Minister when he discussed this question some years ago, and I trust that I am not asking too much when I ask him to put these words into action, with regard to the officials whose conduct it is my intention to bring before the House. The right hon. gentleman then said :
Now. when we find an officer in the ftivil service, however good a servant he may have been, however faithfully he may have discharged his duties, but has been an active politician, who has taken part in the election offensively and actively, and before the eyes of the whole community, that official has become a scandal in the eyes of the community and I have no hesitation in saying that he cannot be trusted to render faithful service to this government. Where there is a government officer he may hold his opinions, I do not care what they are; they may be Liberal, or Conservative, I do not care ; he may go and vote, and I will not inquire how he voted-hut when he is seen on the public platform, when he takes part in party processions and is actively and offensively prominent, that as regards party candidates, that man has taken his life in his hands, and no one can have a word to say if he is dismissed from the service.
These were the remarks of the right hon. gentleman on that occasion, so that if I can produce evidence to satisfy him of the partisanship of officials who are in the employ of his own government to-day, and who have even gone beyond the extent laid down in these declarations of the Prime Minister, I think that we may fairly claim that it is the bounden duty of the government to at once dismiss these officials because of offensive partsanship. The remarks which I have read contain the broad principle laid down by the Prime Minister upon which he intended to guide his future acfions. That principle is; that an official of this government may hold whatever opinions he may desire, and the Prime Minister would not question that; he may exercise his franchise in a quiet} manner and the Prime Minister will not interfere With him, but that official shall not go one step beyond that-in no manner, shape or form shall he actively engage in the public party warfare, or if he does he places his official position in jeopardy. I do not at all suppose that when the right hon. gentleman gave voice to that declaration, he meant it to apply to Conservative officials alone. I will not believe that the Prime Minister would be so unfair as to discriminate in such a manner. I will not believe that he would apply one

of the present government to do active service in my behalf. In due time when my resignation has been handed in, I will then earnestly cooperate with you for the overthrow of the present administration. I trust that since you have shown such confidence in me you will leave nothing undone to ensure my election as your representative.
Yours sincerly,

speechtext: So that if the acting Minister of the Interior desired any evidence of the fact that these gentlemen were candidates, all he had to do was to pick up the Winnipeg ' Free Press,' the organ of the Liberal party in the province of Manitoba, and he would have seen there for the last six weeks a list of the candidates of the party, and figuring conspicuously among them Mr. Young and Mr. Jonasson. It may be that Sir. Young will resign his position during the campaign ; but if so, no doubt the position will be kept open for him until after the election, just as in the case of Mr. Jerome. But fancy Mr. Young attending to his duties during the election, while abstaining from canvassing. This letter was the outcome of the pressure brought to bear upon him by his political friends. He tries to convey the impression that he is not going to engage in canvassing while he holds his office. He hopes to draw his salary until nomination day, and to have the place kept open for him until after the election, in case he should be defeated. No reply that we shall have to-day from the acting Minister of the Interior will be satisfactory to this House, even if we are told that these gentlemen will be notified that they cannot be candidates while they are officers of the government, unless we have the further promise that the public service will not be allowed to suffer by these offices not being filled during the campaign, and that the positions will not be kept open until after the election in order to allow these same gentlemen to drop back into them in return for the sacrifices they are making for their party. I do not think the answer will be satisfactory to the House unless we are told that these gentlemen have to cease at once discharging their duties as officials of this government, or else refuse the nominations of these conventions. This letter was written on April 22nd ; three weeks have elapsed, and still Mr. Young has not been notified to quit his position as an official of this government. When these facts are brought to the attention of the acting Minister of the Interior, he cannot plead ignorance of them. I charge that these gentlemen have been availing themselves of all the prestige conferred upon them by occupying these positions, and have used that fact as a lever to secure votes for themselves and the party to which they belong. The premier of Manitoba, in a public speech delivered in Winnipeg a couple of weeks ago, used the following language in reference to this question :

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext:
I want to draw your attention too, to another hypocritical plank of their platform. They say in clause 10, that they declare in favour of the establishment and maintenance of an efficient and non-partisan civil service. Gentlemen, I agree with that expression of principle. I concur in it and endorse that sentiment, but how do their acts contrast with their professions ? Why in this very day's ' Free Press ' you will find published a list of Liberal candidates who are civil servants, who are paid officials of the Dominion government, and who are using their positions and their power to coerce and influence electors against the Rob-lin government. Only to-day I received information of a homestead inspector, a Dominion government official who is using his official position, whose time is paid for with your money and mine, whose travelling expenses even are paid by the Dominion government, and who is canvassing against the Roblin government amongst farmers who have not taken out their patents, endeavouring by the abuse of his official position to coerce and induce them to vote for the Liberal candidates. Sir, I say that a more scandalous and outrageous abuse of the civil service has never been heard of and cannot exist and cannot be conceived, and I go further and I call upon the independent members of the Dominion parliament, whose servants these men are, to refuse to pass the estimates for the Department of the Interior, to refuse to allow one dollar of public money to be voted for that department, until such men as Jonasson and Jerome and Young and others whom I might name who are receiving large salaries from the federal government, either resign their positions as officials of the Dominion government, or resign as candidates in the Liberal interests in this province.
Here is a strong expression from the premier of the province that the officials of this government are abusing their positions in the interests of the Liberal party. No more glaring instances of partisanship could be brought forward. There have been upwards of 150 dismissals by this government. largely in the Interior and Post Office Departments in Manitoba and Northwest Territories alone. All of these were published in the Conservative organ, in the province of Manitoba, a couple of years ago. And many of these dismissals were made without any charges of partisanship or charges of any kind having been preferred. And in nine out of ten of these cases in which charges of partisanship were made, there was no investigation, and no chance of defence. In my constituency a postmaster was dismissed because lie had acted as returning officer in the election of 1896. Yet here we have a postmaster, Mr. Ira Stratton, in the town of Stonewall, who is at the same time the editor of a Liberal newspaper and secretary of the Liberal Association. If an official. who acted as returning officer in 1896, had to be dismissed on the ground of active partisanship, surely, this man, Mr. Ira Stratton is far more deserving of like treatment. But Mr. Stratton is not the only gentleman who, if the government were consistent, would lose his position. I am not one to take exception to every coun-

try postmaster, who draws a few dollars a year, being debarred from activity in political matters, although many such postmasters have been dismissed on this charge since this government came into power. But let me give the case of a gentleman who holds a rather important postion and is nevertheless an active partisan. In the city of Brandon, where the former postmaster was dismissed on the ground of active partisanship, his successor was present at the convention recently held which selected a Liberal candidate for that constituency. But he can rest perfectly secure because he happens to be a Liberal. Another postmaster named Lawrie, in the town of Morris, acted as presiding officer at the Liberal convention which selected an opponent to the attorney-general of Manitoba. Mr. J. W. Yeo, who is the Dominion lands sub-agent, was also a delegate to a Liberal convention in the province of Manitoba for the selection of a candidate. There are a dozen other postmasters who have been delegates to Liberal conventions. Mr. Charles Tomlin, immigration official, was also a delegate to a Liberal convention. I do not think that the lion. Fostmaster General, who is the acting Minister of the Interior, should hesitate about dealing out severe treatment to these officials, if he proposes to stand by the platform of the Liberal party as formulated in Winnipeg. There was a most curious condition of affairs in that city three or four weeks ago. We had the executive committee, or what is called the ' inner circle ' of Liberals, in that province in convention. A certain number of representatives were appointed to formulate a platform on which the Liberal party would appeal to the country, and what do you think was one of the most important planks in that platform ? It was plank ten :
We declare in favour of the establishment and maintenance of an efficient and non-partisan civil service.
And in that inner circle to which I have referred, there were upwards of a dozen civil servants of this government. Could you conceive anything more hypocritical ? Could you imagine a greater travesty on politeal honesty ? Just imagine these officials of the Dominion government formulating a political platform and declaring themselves in favour of a non-partisan civil service. Further, we had a speech at Brandon by Mr. Greenway, the leader of the Liberal party. In the course of his speech, he was asked this question : ' Are you in favour of a non-partisan civil service ?' He replied : ' Any man who occupies a position in the service of the government, which gives him a livelihood, ought not to meddle in politics at all.' Surely, in view of these declarations of policy, the hon. minister need not hesitate about dismissing these gentlemen or giving them the option either to resign their positions in the service or vacate their positions as nominees of those conventions. I do not know whether the acting Minister of the Interior wants to assume the responsibility or not of doing this. He may possibly think that in so doing he would be trespassing on the preserves of his absent colleague (Hon. Mr. Sifton). But it seems to me that that absent colleague ought to be here attending to the business of parliament. Session after session we find him absenting himself and allowing his place in this House to be taken by somebody else. He has been dubbed by his political admirers 'The Young Napoleon,' but I fail to see any exhibition of Napoleonic capacity or courage when he acts in this manner.
I also wish to point out that there are other officials of this government actively engaged in political warfare. Take Mr. Alfred Martin, who is employed selecting the swamp lands which are to be handed over to the province of Manitoba. Yet, although he is in the employ of this government and paid at the rate of $10 per day, he goes about attending Liberal conventions, proposing Liberal candidates and making partisan speeches. Then there is Mr. Cockburn, who was candidate for North Winnipeg, and who is reported in the press as being the postmaster for the north branch Main street post office in North Winnipeg. I would draw the attention of the hon. Postmaster General to this case.
I have laid these cases, before the Postmaster General, and am not going to enter upon the broad question of dismissals. I have merely specified a few of the more flagrant eases-in Manitoba, concerning which, there is at present, a great deal of adverse criticism, and which demand immediate action on the part of the government. I hardly think that the hon. minister will take the ground that because these men took part in local elections, they have not laid themselves open to action on the part of this government. A partisan is a partisan, and it makes no difference whether he be a partisan in Dominion or in provincial politics. And a man who takes the platform and is offensive to his political opponents, I care not whether lie is engaged in Dominion or provincial politics, and is at the same time a civil servant, should be forced to vacate one position or the other. And, in saying this, I desire to state also that I shall not be satisfied with a mere promise on the part of the government which will allow these gentlemen to drop out of their positions and have those positions kep/t open for them to be taken by them after the elections are over. This is what happened] in the constituency of Marquette, in the Dominion elections of 1900. Mr. .lolm W. Thompson was homestead inspector. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) attended the convention that selected this official of liis department as the candidate of his party to oppose myself. It is true that Mr. Thompsou resigned his position, but that position was kept open for him, and

when he had been buried under an avalanche of votes-I think the majority against him was 420-he was reinstated, and for over two years has been discharging the duties of that position. That is exactly what we expect will be the case with the officials whose cases are brought forward to-day; and I do not think there is any lion, gentleman in the House who will defend such an action on the part of the government. Therefore, I desire to move the following amendment :
That all the words after ' that ' in the proposed motion he left out and the following substituted therefor :-
The Prime Minister speaking in this House on the 1st day of September, A.D. 1896, with respect to political partisanship by officers of the government expressed himself as follows :
' Now, when we find an officer in the civil service, however good a servant he may have been, however faithfully he may have discharged his duties, bun who has been an active politician, who has taken part in the election offensively and actively, and before the eyes of the whole community, that official has become a scandal in the eyes of the community, and I have no hesitation in saying that he cannot be trusted to render faithful service to this government. Where there is a government officer he may hold his opinions, I do not care what they are ; they may be Liberal or Conservative, I do not care ; he may go and vote, and I will not inquire how he voted-but when he is seen on the public platform, when he takes part in party processions and is actively and offensively prominent as regards party candidates, that man has taken his life in his hands, and no one can have a word to say if he is dismissed from the service.'
The Minister of Trade and Commerce on the same day used the following language in speaking on the same subject :-[DOT]
' With members of the civil service eating the bread of both parties and deliberately interfering with the elections for the purpose of aiding one political party, if they so act they must be considered as taking their political lives in their hands and they must accept the consequences of their own acts, and the good sense of the people of the country and their natural sense of equal justice will not merely justify but demand at the hands of the government that they should make an example of them.'
That other members of the government during that session and in subsequent sessions expressed the same views.
That the government acting upon the principles and rules so laid down has since dismissed a very large number of officers on the ground of alleged political partisanship.
That an application of the principles and rules so laid down for the guidance of public officials would result in the dismissal of those officers of the government who have become ' a scandal in the eyes of the community ' by taking an active offensive and partisan part in the election campaign now being carried on in the province of Manitoba, and who while ' eating the bread of both parties ' are ' deliberately interfering in elections for the purpose of aiding one political party.'
This House regrets that the government has not seen fit to deal with such officials in accordance with the declarations of principle so made and so often acted upon.

MeCREARY (Selkirk). Mr. Speaker, before this question is decided, 1 desire, as one of the members from Manitoba to say a few words in reference to it. In any reply I may make to the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), I shall not condone the offence of a civil servant taking an active part in politics. But when the hon. gentleman commences to lecture this House, and to declare the action of civil servants in Manitoba a public scandal, he is the last man who should speak in this way, and he comes from the province which is the last province from which charges against this government should come. For, if there is one province in confederation where the civil servants have been open partisans, where they have been active election agents, it is the province of Manitoba. Before proceeding to deal witn the question generally, I may deal with the case of the officials he specifically mentioned. The first is the case of Mr. Martin Jerome, a homestead inspector and an efficient officer. It is true, he Has been a member of the local House for the last four years. But it is not fair to speak of Mr. Jerome as being in active politics. He is not to-day a likely candidate for the local House in that province, but is entirely out of politics so far as that is concerned. Before I go further, I may say that there is precedent for Mr. Jerome's action. It is a well known fact that many members of the local legislatures of Canada have been men receiving salaries from the Dominion government. During the time when Sir Adolphe Caron was Postmaster General, it is a well known fact, many of the postmasters were members of the local legislatures of their respective provinces. But we do not need to go to other provinces for precedent in this matter. Take the present provincial secretary and Minister of Public Works of the province of Manitoba, Hon. D. II. McFadden. We find that he, while a member of the local House, for many years was employed by the Dominion government as veterinary inspector at Emerson, from 1884 to 1897. During that time he successfully contested provincial seats in 1892 and 1896. This was during the term of office in the Dominion of hon. gentlemen opposite. There is also the case of Mr. Baldwinson, who for the last four years has been representative of the constituency of Gimli in the local House. That gentleman was employed by the late government as Icelandic immigration commissioner at Winnipeg, from 1883 to 1889. On March 25th, 18S9, his salary was increased from $730 to $830, showing that they actually rewarded him by an increase of salary for having become a member of the local house. Now it is not necessary for me to go further. I could mention half a dozen gentlemen who were earning salaries from this government while they were still members of the local house during the Conservative regime. Wm. Wagner

and Wm. Crawford, for eight or ten years swamp-land commissioner under this government were members of the local house and received good salaries. Not only that, but they had not even the decency to resign their positions as land commissioners while parliament was in session. Take Hugh John Macdonald's case. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite will say that he should be a man above reproach, that he should not violate the civil service rule, yet we find that that gentleman was premier and railway commissioner for many months, from January 11,1899, up to October, in 1900. I do not know that I have any right to give away secrets of that kind. The hon. gentleman threw out the wrong hook. Now, Mr. Speaker, in regard to postmasters taking an active part in politics, I think the contention of the hon. gentleman is ridiculous. He did not go so far to-day as his brief in the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' allowed him to go. They say that postmasters who draw $12 a year should not take an active part in politics, that census enumerators who two years ago received $7 or $8 for service rendered should be prevented from taking an active part in politics. I submit that their contention is ridiculous. I presume that when a man is in the civil service ou the permanent list and is in receipt of a large salary he should not take an active part in politics. I have been a civil servant myself for three years and a half and I faithfully observed that rule, and no charge was ever made against me. I submit that that rule should be carried out to-day; but when you ask that a man who is receiving a small salary of $7 or $8 or $12 a year as postmaster to refrain from taking an active part in provincial politics, why the idea is ridiculous. The hon. gentleman mentioned such names as Stratton, of Stonewall: Cockburn, of North Winnipeg; Laurie, of Morris, and others, men who receive actually no emolument whatever from the Dominion government. It is true their names stand there as holders of offices, but they pay out in expenses more than the Post Office Department allows them, because they have stores in these places and they are the most convenient places for the public to go to get their mail.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if I were disposed to enter into an argument on this matter, I think I could furnish some interesting reading to the members of the House, because if there is any province in which the civil service law has been abused it is the province of Manitoba. The hon. gentleman has said that there were about 150 dismissals in Manitoba and the North-west Territories by this government since they came into power. But would you believe it, Sir, that the Conservative government of the province of Manitoba, since coming into power on the 11th day of January, 1900, have made 700 dismissals in that province ? I have before me a list of them, it is two years old, two years since I obtained it, but if I were to read that list it would afford interesting information to this House. On the 11th of January, Hugh John Macdonald was sworn in as minister, and on the 22nd of January the mill commenced to grind on the poor Grits. On that day we find the guillotine was applied to Mr. Howrie, game warden, and Mr. A. Taylor was appointed in his place. There was a lull in the proceedings for a few days and on the 7th of February we find the mill began to grind again, and on that day there were some ten or twelve dismissals of men against whom there was no cause of complaint. I have here some of them. Mr. W. E. Perdue, ' guardian ad litem,' was dismissed. He was a gentleman of considerable influence, a prominent barrister of Winnipeg, and he was dismissed. D. W. McKercher, another prominent barrister, was dismissed as official administrator, also S. R. Wright, D. W. McKercher and R. M. Matheson, official administrators, all dismissed without any cause ; Mr. G. Thorsteinsson, police magistrate of Gimli, was dismissed on that day; the bailiff of the county court, A. M. Livingstone, was dismissed. D. Philip, chief clerk of the provincial secretary and Queen's printer, was dismissed on that day. [DOT]T. W. Sifton, father of the Minister of the Interior, was dismissed from the Public Works Department and on the same day .T. A. McDonnell was dismissed from the position of engineer. I have column after column of names of gentlemen who were dismissed within a few months after the advent of the Conservative government. There was Mr. .Tames Thompson, clerk of the timber office, Winnipeg. There was Mr. S. A. D. Bertrand, who was official assignee for the province, dismissed by that government on February 7, and F. J. Nixon, a strong partisan, was appointed in his place. So indignant were the public over that dismissal and appointment that the wholesale

inen and the board of trade called a meeting of both sides of politics and threw the appointment back into the face of the premier and said they would give no estates to be handled by any such assignee as that. When the hon. gentleman talks about the civil service of Manitoba he talks to one who knows something about it. Now, coming down to the town of Nepawa, we find on tile same day, February 7, less than thirty days after they took power, that Mr. .Tames Thompson was dismissed and R. C. Ennis was put in his place. We find that T. A. Cuddy was dismissed as clerk of the county court of Minnedosa and J. F. Boyd was put in his place. Perhaps the hon. gentleman knows about that.
Mr, ROCHE (Marquette). I deny it.
Mr. McCreary. Mr. J. M. Robinson, burser of the Brandon asylum, was dismissed and E. Hughes put in his place. E. C. Conklin, clerk of the legislative assembly, was dismissed and A. H. Corelli was put in his place.	Mr. Charles Smith
was dismissed as shorthand reporter. Mr. N. Todd was dismissed as bailiff of the county court of St. Francios Xavier, and J. Bourke was put in his place. In fact from the 7th of February to six months afterwards I find that there were dismissed some ninety or one hundred civil servants in the province of Manitoba, some four hundred and forty-one justices of the peace, and over one hundred game guardians. In that one little province alone, six or seven hundred officers were dismissed during six months. The axe was ground up and it was put to work. They have a very peculiar way of dismissing civil servants up there. I do not blame Mr. Hugh .Tohn Macdonald so much. Any one who knows the inside reasons for his resigning from the position of prime minister of Manitoba, knows why he got out. There is what we call the Maple Leaf Conservative Club. It is an institution composed of nearly 3.000 members, and I know something of its methods, because I am able to keep pretty closely in touch with it. It has ramifications all through the province and it has an inner circle of nine in Winnipeg, which is a kind of Clan-na-Gael society. This inner circle meets in secret conclave and decides what heads shall be cut off the following day. It makes a list, sends that list up to the premier, and if the premier does not promptly cut off these heads and appoint other men in their places, he gets notice that the secret conclave is going to go back on him. I happen to know that that occurred in at lieast two cases which came upder my notice. One case is that of Dr. Patterson. Dr. Patterscn was a most capable official under the former Manitoba government. He was a great personal friend of Mr. Hugh John Macdonald, being his next door neighbour for many years, and I happen to know that the day before Dr. Patterson was dismissed he was told by Mr. Macdonald himself that he was
Mr. McCreary.
all right, that he had taken no active part in politics except to cast his vote and that his position would not be disturbed. That night, when the secret conclave met, that position was required for another partisan of the Maple Leaf Clan-na-Gael society, and down went the axe. I can mention another case, that of Ami Freeman, a poor Icelandic boy who came out to this country about twenty-five years ago, and who, although a cripple, was able to earn sufficient money to educate himself. He was employed in the license department and although he was taking no active part in politics and had been assured that lie would not be disturbed in his position, he was dismissed. At four o'clock, before he quitted his office on a certain day, he got a letter from Mr. Macdonald in answer to one that he had written, stating that he would not be disturbed in his position, but that night the Clan-na-Gael met in secret conclave, Freeman's head was required and next morning at eleven o'clock he received a letter from Mr. Macdonald saying that lie was dismissed. All that correspondence can be brought to the attention of the House if necessary. It ill becomes the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) to stand up and talk about civil servants in the province of Manitoba. The right hon. leader of the government knows very well that I personally went to him to tell him of the position of affairs that existed in Manitoba, and how men were being deposed from their positions to make room for needy partisans of the present government of Manitoba. Men who had come into Manitoba in 1870 with Wolseley and who held small positions bringing them $200 or $300 a year with which to maintain themselves in their old age, were dismissed from their places. These men were dismissed without cause. I only trust that this government will take the matter up and deal with these officials as they should deal with them, if they looked at it from a purely party spirit. I want to pay this measure of credit to the right lion, leader of the government, that I went to his private office and complained bitterly of the treatment that some of these men had received at the hands of the present government of Manitoba. His answer was: They are making a mistake, they are violating the principles of constitutional government, but, because they do wrong, would you ask me to do likewise ? I said : No, sir. Probably if I had gone a little farther there might have been a difference, but I did not choose to do so. I claim that the Roblin government have, during the short time which they have been in office, done more to disorganize the civil service of Manitoba than any government in any province since confederation. I do not intend to deal very fully with this matter because there may be some other western members who know a good deal about the civil service of the west. I can remember the time in Mani-

toba and the North-west Territories when a man's life was not safe if he dared to say a word against the Conservative party. I can remember that during the election of 1887 the number of civil servants imported into the city of Winnipeg to vote was far more than the majority that the member elected got at that time, and there are cases in the Territories much worse than that. The hon. gentleman has also mentioned certain civil servants and for liis edification I will just call his attention to a few officers under Mr. Roblin's administration who are taking an active part in provincial elections. Take the case of R. G. O'Malley, who formerly was a member of the local house. He is what is called the noxious weed inspector. During the election of 1900, when I had the honour of being a candidate in the constituency of Selkirk, Mr. O'Malley was the official organizer against me in that constituency. He followed me all over. There was a little snow and ice on the ground. I met him in the parish of St. Laurent. When I reached there O'Malley was there and the first man that X had to speak against at the meeting was R. G. O'Malley, provincial noxious weed inspector. I said : Mr. O'Malley are you finding any noxious weeds here or noxious Grits, while going around here on skates or snowshoes ? With the aid of a priest in the parish they thought they were going to defeat me, but I was able for the first time in the history of the parish to get a Liberal majority of eighteen. We also had this gentleman just a very few days ago. Mr. Speaker, getting up in a public meeting in Assiniboia and making a strong political speech ; in fact, from the time of the man's appointment down to the present he has been doing nothing but acting as the organizer of the local government. That is his business. Rut. there are others. There is Mr. Joseph Burke, if you please, a so-called immigration agent of the Manitoba government. Mr. Burke, accidentally, so they put it, slipped up to the parish of St. Claude ostensibly to look after some immigrants to be transferred to another portion of the province, and we have him on political platforms making strong political speeches, in fact the speech of the day. There is Mr. Patenaude, another gentleman who has been appointed an immigration agent, is actually the organizer in Assiniboia for Mr. Caron. Then there is J. J. Golden, another gentleman appointed as an immigrant agent, and who was sent to Kansas for a short time, but who was brought back and is now an active politician in Winnipeg. There is not a single immigration official that they have appointed, and they have appointed probably twenty-five or thirty, who is not appointed absolutely for the purpose of doing canvassing work in Manitoba during the elections. We have another case, that of the police magistrate of Winnipeg-Mr. Dawson. Mr. Dawson was a most capable official. He has been a lawyer of high standing and he held a high place in the estimation of every barrister of Winnipeg, lie is a man who had never taken an active part in politics, but this inner circle of nine wanted his place for a member of the association, Mr. Baker. Off went Mr. Dawson's head, and Mr. Baker was appointed to take his place on the bench. But, matters became a little too hot for Mr. Roblin. A petition, signed by the citizens of Winnipeg, was sent to Mr. Roblin and things have become so hot that he would be glad to get Mr. Baker out of it, were it not for the pressure of the Clan-na-Gael that I speak of.
This Clan-na-Gael; this inner circle of the Maple I.eaf Conservatives of Winnipeg, is rather peculiarly constituted. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House will wonder how I got possession of this information, but I did. A man goes in there and he is given a ticket, with his number on it ; nothing else but the number. He is asked to subscribe to a declaration extending over two sheets of typewritten foolscap, and he promises that he will, during the time he belongs to that institution, do all in his power to oust any Liberal from any job, whether it is in the employ of the municipality or the government. He declares that he will do all in his power, if employed as subordinate, to oust the foreman, if the foreman is a Liberal ; and that he will do all in his power to bring party politics into municipal, provincial or Dominion affairs or anything else. That is the state of thing we have to fight against in the city of Winnipeg. That is the institution which has Mr. Roblin by the neck, and forces him to make some of these dismissals and some of these appointments X have spoken of. Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) say that this state of affairs is a public scandal in the province of Manitoba ? What does he think now of the officials in the employment of his own government and not of the Dominion government ?
