Sir. SIcCREARY. High binders of the worst kind. I could, Sir. Speaker, at considerable length give the names of I.iberal officials who have been dismissed by the Slanitoba Conservative government, but I think the House is in possession of sufficient facts to warrant it in saying that if there is a mistake made by one of the officials in this government-and I believe that some officials have gone too far in the province of Slanitoba-still it ill-becomes the hou. gentleman (Sir. Roche), who comes from the province of Slanitoba. to bring these matters up here, when such a condition of affairs exists within the home of his own political party in his own province.

speakeroldname: Sir. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext:
I have listened attentively to the joint speech of the members for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) and Saskatchewan (Sir.

Davis), and they have said nothing particularly which prevents me from expecting that they will both vote for this amendment. Everything they have said shows that there is a great grievance in this country, and more particularly in Manitoba than any other part of the Dominion, which requires the remedy proposed by this motion. Should the government decide to reject the amendment moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Roche), it will be another instance of their breaking one of the pledges they gave to this country. And, Sir, they will break that pledge apparently without any expectation on the part of their followers that it would not be broken. These two gentlemen, whose joint speech we have listened to from the other side, gave us no opinion as to whether they would vote for or against the motion. The member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) simply confined himself to giving instances of the dismissal of public servants for offensive partisanship by the present government of Manitoba, but let me point out that my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) does not say that it is right for a Conservative administration to dismiss Liberal officials, or that a Liberal administration should dismiss Conservative officials. What the hon. gentleman from Marquette (Mr. Roche) has said, and what he puts in his motion is, that the interference of civil service appointees in political issues is a scandal upon the country. My hon. friend (Mr. Roche) quoted the language of the Prime Minister and the language of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in support of his motion, and in condemnation of the very thing that he condemns. The hon. gentleman from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) has taken good care to say that these two ministers were right in stating that such a thing is a scandal, but he intimates nevertheless that this scandal will be allowed to continue in the province of Manitoba.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext: I did not say that at all.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext: That is the inference we must draw from his argument.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext:
The argument that was made by the member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) showed clearly that this government, in 1890, laid down a platform upon this question, containing the rule of conduct for officials therein described, and that this platform has been deliberately broken by the government for three years past. We are here to-day asking that this government should enforce the rule laid down in 1896, or at least explain to the House why they do not enforce it. The right hon. the Prime Minister told us in 1890 :
When we find an officer in the civil service, however good a servant he may have been, however faithfully he may have discharged his duties, but who has been an active politician, Mr. LANCASTER.
who has taken part in the election offensively and actively, and before the eyes of the whole community that official has become a scandal in the eyes of the community.
Now, the country supposes that the Prime Minister meant what he then said, and we are calling attention to the fact that the rule which he announced has not been carried out, and we ask that a remedy shall be applied. It is charged here, and the member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), who knows more about the details than I do, does not deny the facts in regard to these three gentlemen who are named in the motion. Let us see what their conduct has been individually. Mr. Martin Jerome was employed by the Department of the Interior, and the Minister of the Interior told us in this House that if he accepted the Liberal nomination his employment under this government would cease. Well, Mr. Jerome did accept the nomination and he remained for three years a member of the local legislature, and his employment under the federal government did not cease. If a member of parliament or of the legislature is not an active politician, I do not know who is. I do not know that we can find fault with any one saying that the members elected to this House are active politicians, and so with the members of the legislatures, and if the Prime Minister did not intend his description of active politicians to apply to members supporting a political party in parliament, I presume that he would have said so. I think we are entitled to consider a member of the legislature as being an active politician. This Mr. Jerome remained an active politician and a member of the legislature for three years, and also an employee of this government. Is it possible that the government did not know it, or is it that the government simply trusted to luck that no one would draw their attention to it, or find fault with them for ignoring the policy laid down by the Premier on the 1st of September, 1896. The hon. gentleman from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) says that this cannot be called a scandal because Mr. Jerome is now going out, and is about ceasing to be an active politician. Well, what about the scandal during the three years he was a member of the legislature ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) has told us that he has made representations to the government with regard to some other men, but I wonder why he did not have a conversation with the Prime Minister in regard to Mr. Jerome, in which he would tell him that Mr. Jerome was a flagrant example of the disregard of the policy which the government promised to pursue in this matter. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) says that the Premier told him when lie complained of the conduct of the Manitoba government : If they are doing so they are doing wrong; they are false to the principle of constitutional government, and you would not ask me to do the same thing. Why did not

the member for Selkirk say to the Premier : What about the constitutional question, when you have laid down a policy in this connection which you are violating deliberately ?
It strikes me that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) who, we know, is not a forgetful man, who is in no sense an unwise man, who is well able to defend anything he has in mind, and who is, I hope, an honourable man; should at once have taken the position that the honour of the province of Manitoba was at stake, and should have said to the Prime Minister: It is not enough to say that the Conservative government did what was wrong; that is no reason why a Liberal government should do this thing; we have had this public official in the legislature for three years, and what are you going to do about that ? The hon. member does not say that he even mentioned this matter to the Premier. Therefore we must think that he did not consider it a violation of principle on the part of the government to lay down the platform they did in 1896, immediately on coming to power, and to allow abuses of this kind to go on contrary to that principle. I wish now for a moment to answer the reference made by the hon. member for Selkirk to the much respected Hugh John Macdonald. The hon. member said that the name of Hugh John Macdonald was above reproach. I want to ask him the reason for that. It is because when Hugh John Macdonald made pledges he kept them ; when he laid down a policy, he carried it out. We have an evidence of that in dealing with the prohibition question in Manitoba. If I know anything of human nature, if there is one reason more than another why the people of Manitoba on both sides of politics hold the name of Hugh John Macdonald above reproach, it is because when he made a pledge, he carried out that pledge on attaining power. I do not think that backhanded compliment to this government ought to have come from one of their own supporters. I would have thought it would have been left for one of us on this side of the House. It is true, we on this side of the House have dealt with matters of this kind so many times that the hon. member for Selkirk may have thought that our power had been used up in pointing out so many broken pledges and that we would not again bring up this question of the government breaking their pledges, the good province of Manitoba may have thought it well to have one of the Liberal members take it up. They need not be afraid, however, because the members of the opposition, in their duty to the country, will endeavour to have some of these evils remedied. Now, we have had quoted to us the language of the right hon. the Premier, on this question; we have also had quoted the language of his left hand partner, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who spoke as follows
in regard to members of the civil service taking part in elections :
With those examples before us, yea, with members of the civil service eating the bread of both parties, and deliberately interfering in elections for the purpose' of aiding one political party, if they so act they must be considered as taking their political lives in their hands, and they must accept the consequences of their own acts, and the good sense of the people of the country and their natural sense of equal justice will not merely justify, but demaud at the hands of the government that they should make an example of them.
We have also bad the language of Sir Louis Davies, then a member of the cabinet, quoted by the hon. member for Marquette in the same sense. The hon. gentleman then a member of this government went the length of saying that the principle should be applied to men who interfere against the opposition as well as to men who interfere against the government-that it should be applied to all officials who interfered in any way in political matters. I do not think there can be any question that the principle should be applied to men of both political parties; and I do not expect that the government will take the strong hint given to them by the hon. member for Selkirk, and assert that a Conservative official who interferes in elections does wrong, while the Liberal official who interferes does not do wrong. I want to draw the attention of the government, in the interest of the country, to what is going to be the result if they treat this matter as a huge joke, or pass it over lightly, under the impression that no one is going to pay much attention to it. I ask them to consider if they are not doing much greater harm to the rising generation of this country by laying down these principles and pledges and then refusing to notice any violations of them than they would do by raising a duty higher than they think they should, or putting a duty lower than they think they should. It is not only tariffs or readjusting constituencies, or whether a railway commission should be appointed or not, or how much money should be spent on public works, that this House has to concern itself with. But here is a government just fresh from the country laying down the principles that ought to govern in these matters; and here is an hon. gentleman, the member for Marquette, who knows what he is talking about, who has never been known to misjudge anything stated in this House, who is noted for. carefulness in his statements, giving three specific instances of absolute violations of these principles which were thus laid down by this government. Now, we have not yet heard from the government on the subject. I would have thought that immediately on the hon. member for Marquette resuming his seat, some member of the government would have paid, not the hon. member for Marquette but the country whom they

serve, the courtesy of stating what they thought about it. They seem to think their followers from Manitoba should answer the hon. member for Marquette; but I wish to tell them that this matter is not confined to the province of Manitoba. 1 ask them to pay the province of Ontario the courtesy of explaining what this platform meant, of saying wherein we have misconstrued it, of showing wherein the three cases mentioned by the hon. member for Marquette are not applicable to the platform as laid down by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The government are not obliged to do so; but I warn them that if they think the province of Ontario is not interested in this matter, because it only happened in Manitoba, or is going to treat it lightly, they are greatly mistaken, and they ought to put themselves right before the province and before the whole Dominion. There are words in this resolution which do not appear to me to be capable of any two meanings; but I know that this government has often been able to show that things did not mean what the country thought they did. I appeal to the government to let us know distinctly and clearly what those words do mean, and wherein the cases cited by the hon. member for Marquette are not applicable. If they are applicable, let the government not be satisfied with saying that some Conservative government did worse at some other time; because that is not the question. I am not admitting or denying that they did. We are dealing with the present administration. Although the hon. member for Selkirk said that Conservative governments in the past had done the same thing or allowed it to be done. I want to point out this great moral and national difference between the two governments in that respect; that the Conservative government never made a pledge on the subject and broke it, while this government did. It does not matter, for the purpose of this argument, or his motion, whether the Conservative government did wrong or not, but it does matter whether the government of this country keeps its pledges on not. The difference between the two parties is this :	No Conservative government has ever been shown to have laid down within the four walls, of this House any speech or policy or pledge like this one made by this government. No Conservative government has ever been known to break its pledges, and then, when called to task, try to laugh the charges away, regardless to what the people may think. But just the contrary is the course fallowed by this Liberal government. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen opposite to say that it does not lie in the mouths of Conservative members to raise this question, but that answer will not go down to the people. It lies in the mouths of Conservative members to do their duty. It matters not whether the Conservative party did wrong eight or Mr. LANCASTER.
ten years ago-and I am not admitting that they did-that is not the question at issue now. We are dealing with matters of the present. AVe are dealing with the present administration and calling it to account for its failure to carry out its pledges. These pledges and principles are well laid down in the speeches of the right hon. the First Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and Sir Louis Davies, and the cases cited of Thompson, Young, Jonassen and Jerome, prove conclusively what little respect this government has for the pledges on which it secured public support, and until it can be shown that these cases are not in direct violation of the platform thus laid down by the Liberal party. I shall support the amendment of my hon. friend from Marquette.
Mr. AA\ SCOTT (AVest: Assinibcia). The position taken by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken is a most, convenient one for his party. He has laid down the doctrine that the Conservative party is perfectly free to do wrong, because it never pledged itself to do right.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext: I did not say anything of the kind.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has pronounced an eulogium very well deserved on the whole, of Mr. Hugh John Macdonald, of Manitoba, and then proceeded to say that the Conservative party had never made a pledge which it did not keep. This will be news to this House. Why, before the last local election in Manitoba there was given to the people on the authority of Mr. Hugh John Macdonald a platform consisting of nineteen planks, and one of those planks bound the Conservative party to keep politics out of the administration of justice. Yet Mr. Hugh John Macdonald had only been in power a few weeks when he cut the official heads off 450 justices of the peace, and replaced them by 450 Tories. On this side we have no objection to make to the advertisement of Mr. Macdonald as a gentleman who always keeps his word, but whenever that picture is held out to us, it brings to our minds those celebrated nineteen planks in the Conservative platform of December, 1899, and the fact that not one of these planks was ever adhered to. My hon. friend referred to the question of prohibition, which reminds us that although Mr. Hugh John Macdonald promised that if elected he would give the province a prohibitory law. that promise remains still unfulfilled. He also promised that the number of cabinet ministers would be reduced from five to three, yet still we have five. He further pledged himself and his party to reduce the indemnity of the members of the legislature from $500 to $300, yet the very next session they were paid an indemnity of $600. I happen to have the misfortune of living in a part of the country which is not yet a province, but

only a territory, and possibly I do not quite understand the force of the argument made by lion, gentlemen opposite regarding civil servants. I have not been favoured either with a copy of the amendment which has been put into your hands, Mr. Speaker, by the hon. member for Marquette, but if I understand his complaint, it is this, that the three gentlemen whom he named, and who are Dominion government officials, have been candidates for the Manitoba legislature. I would ask my hon. friend if that is correct ?

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext: I think that there were more than three, but I mentioned three, Young, Jonasson and Watson, postmaster of South Brandon, though I am not sure whether I mentioned Mr. Watson or not. But I did not mention one-third of those I could have.

maintopic: THOS YOUNG.
speechtext:
It may be because I live in a territory and not in a province that I fail to see the reason of the complaint. In the North-west we have not yet introduced federal politics into local affairs. As I understand it, the pledge given by leaders of the Liberal party had reference to the interference of government officials in federal politics and had nothing to do with local politics. At all events, that is my understanding of it, and so far as I have heard no attempt has been made to prove interference in federal politics against these gentlemen. I am disposed to question whether it is proper for this House to lay down the principle that Dominion officials have not the right to exercise their franchise, and even take the platform in provincial elections, provided that it does not interfere with their duties as officers of this government.
I would not be disposed to take the position that these servants of the Dominion government have not a perfect right to take part in provincial elections. I know very well-and I think the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Muloek) will bear me out-that some of the postmasters of the North-west Territories are actually members of the local legislature. I can cite one instance-the member of the local legislature for the constituency of White wood, who was the postmaster at that point, and, I think, is yet, and, at the present time, is deputy speaker of the local legislature of the North-west Territories. However, 1 would not care to go very far in laying down a position on this subject. I merely wish to say, in support of what has been so very well and forcibly said by my hon. friend from Selkirk, that tlie Conservatives in the province of Manitoba and the North-west Territories are the very last people in the world who have any call or any right to make complaints in this matter. Anybody who knows the conditions which prevailed in the province of Manitoba and the North-west
Territories for the years from the opening of that country up to 1896, knows very well the tyranny [DOT] practiced by the government through its officials in that country. Until 1896, it was never possible for a Liberal to be elected in that country, except on one occasion. And one fact referred to by the hon. member for Marquette, the fact that liis opponent in the last election had been a Dominion official. Mr. Thompson, a homestead inspector, proved, as well as anything could prove, the difference in the conditions which prevail now from those which prevailed prior to that time. For, up to 1896, while the Conservative government was in power in the Dominion, if an official had taken a nomination on behalf of the Conservative party there is no human power that could have been used by the Liberal party that would have resulted in the defeat of that Conservative candidate. My hon. friend from Marquette also complained of the difference between the treatment that is meted out by this government to officials who happen to be Liberals and that meted out to officials who happen to be Conservatives. Well, I have some knowledge, so far as the territories are concerned at all events, of the conduct of government affairs, and, so far as I have been able to see, there is no difference in the treatment meted out by the various ministers to the officials, whether those officials are Conservatives or Liberals. But I may say that, prior to the Liberal government coming into power in 1896, the lists of civil servants in Manitoba and the North-west Territories might have been searched from tots to bottom without discovering a sign of a single Liberal in that service. My hon. friend referred to a long list of officials who, he alleged, had been dismissed by this government since 1896. I suppose he had the old Winnipeg' ' Telegram' list as a basis for his statement. 1 recollect very well that some time ago the Winnipeg * Telegram ' gave what purported to be a full list of the officials dismissed by this government in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Trobably the hon. gentleman was correct when he placed the number at one hundred and fifty. But I recollect also, very distinctly that when 1 went over the list' I found the names of men who had died while in office, as well as the names of others who had left the service of their own volition, either to go into other lines of business or, perhaps, to leave the part of the country where they had been residing. When I analysed the list, to find the basis for these charges of wholesale dismissal of officials, I found that there was only about 25 per cent of the 'Telegram's' list who had actually been dismissed, and in all of those cases concerning which I had personal information, there was very good reason for dismissal. In most cases there had been charges formally or informally made and an investigation held, which, revealed

facts fully justifying tlie dismissal. My bon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) who hist spoke, laid down a doctrine which, if the proposal which my hon. friend from Marquette asks the House to accept, were accepted, would be most convenient for the Conservative party in Manitoba. The result would be that this government would immediately put chains on every Liberal official in the country, preventing them from taking any part in politics, from exerting any influence or, probably, even from casting their votes, while at the same time, every local Conservative official appointed by the Rolilin government would be free to go up and down the country, as my hon. friend from Selkirk says they have been doing, exercising all possible influence in the elections soon to be held.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have one other matter which is not distinctly germane to this matter which I wish to mention. It relates to the discussion which took place here last night. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), in referring to a gentleman who made one of the statutory declarations which I read before the House, Mr. Trant, of Regina, stated that that gentleman was a civil servant, this being stated to give special weight to charges against him. I may say that Mr. Trant is not a civil servant in the ordinary sense of the term. A most disagreeable reference was made by my hon. friend from Peel to Mr. Trant, and I wish to occupy two minutes in making a statement in reference to that gentleman, as I intended to do last night, but was prevented. Mr. Trant has a reputation, and, like the rest of us, no doubt, is anxious to uphold that reputation. Mr. Trant spends part of his time in performing the duties of secretary to the Lieutenant Governor in Regina. When the party of the hon. leader of the opposition visited Regina, Mr. Trant, who represents the ' Free Press ' of Winnipeg-

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that has engaged a portion of the time of the House this afternoon has been so fully, and I think, so fairly laid before the House that my mission here is a somewhat light one, and if I am to reply to the criticisms of my hon. friends from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) and from West Assini-boia (Mr. Scott) my task wUl not be a difficult one in that respect either. I think the House will agree with me that they have not dealt with the question and that the matters which they have brought to the attention of the House will not make the position of the Liberal party any easier or place it in any better position before the country thau it was before they addressed the House. Now, the question is this :	The Liberal
party has laid down, as has been shown by the quotations which have been read from the speeches of the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his lieutenants, the platform that we supposed was to be for the guidance of the party and of all government officials in the country in future. Yet, here we have, in the face of that, no less than, I understand, seven gentlemen, employees of J:he Dominion government, who have accepted nominations as Liberal candidates in the

approaching elections in the province of Manitoba.
The only excuse made by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) is the old excuse which we hear from the other side of the House repeatedly ; that tu quoque argument which is now so well known : Well, when your party was in power you did as bad or worse than we are doing. That is the answer from the Liberal benches to the majority of the charges against this government that we bring to the attention of the country. We do not forget what the Liberals promised before they got into power; we know the pledges they made to the public ; we know the criticisms they levelled against the Conservative government, and we know how they pledged themselves that when they got into power they would redress the alleged grievances against which they protested. But is it not a strange thing to see those gentlemen to-day, now that they have attained power, perpetuating in an intensified form that which they protested against when in opposition. The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) as well as the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) told us that Mr. Jerome had not been a partisan. In order to show that these gentlemen are entirely mistaken about Mr. Jerome's character in that regard, I refer them to a letter which he wrote to the ' Free Press ' on the 30th September last. I shall not weary the House by reading that letter, but suffice it to say that Mr. Jerome takes up a column of the ' Free Press ' in criticising severely the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) who was then a minister of the Liberal government, but who was reported at the time to be not in accord with his colleagues. This would show that Mr. Jerome is so intensely partisan that he is not satisfied with attacking the Conservatives, but that he is prepared to have a fling at even a Liberal minister whose Liberalism is not up to Mr. Jerome's standard. Permit me, Sir, to give a few instances which will explain to hon. gentlemen who do not, perhaps, understand the workings of things in the west, how these officials can exercise considerable power over the voters at the time of an election. These three gentlemen :	Mr. Young, Mr. Jonasson and
Mr. Jerome, in the discharge of theii; duties, visit those who have homesteads or who get permission from the government to cut timber. They are in a position to hold forth the possibility of what they can do and what they may do in their official capacity if those people do not vote in the interest of the party they desire them to. An official in that position may, for a year or more, prevent a man from getting his homestead to which he is entitled, by saying that the settler had not quite complied with all the conditions of the Dominion Lands Act. The timber agent might, if he were so disposed, wield a great influence over the electorate, because he might say to a settler :	you
have cut a few poles more than you are entitled to, and under the power I possess I can punish you for so doing. I have a letter here from the premier of Manitoba, who says that an Icelandic settler came to him making a complaint that he had attended a public meeting which was addressed by Mr. Jonasson, and that the whole trend of that timber agent's speech was to the effect, that in the position he occupied he had the power to confer benefits on those of the electors who did his bidding. At that meeting it is alleged that Mr. Jonasson refused to permit any person to reply on behalf of the Conservative government of Manitoba. These few instances go to show the influence that such officials may use on the electors in that country. In addition to that, these men can go around campaigning and using the government money which is allowed them for expenses in doing so. The hon. gentleman from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) and from the West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) have adduced as a sort of rebuttal evidence, the allegation that when the Conservatives were in power they did as bad or worse than the Liberals are now doing, and if the government is going to rely on such an argument as that, here and now is the place for them to say so. But what took place from 1896, when the Conservative party went out of power in the Dominion, until 1900, when the Manitoba Conservative government was returned. I have here a list of 150 Conservative employees who were dismissed by the present government of the Dominion during the period I have referred to, and before the Manitoba Conservative government came into power. And, Sir, if the Manitoba Conservatives, as has been alleged by the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary), did retaliate, it was, what to some extent might have been expected in view of the dismissal of these 150 Conservative officials, the majority of whom were able and efficient officers, against whom not the slightest charge could be made. I am sure that the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) will not say that Mr. H. H. Smith, who was Land Commissioner for many years was not well qualified to hold his office, and was a man against whom no just charge could be made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: He was not dismissed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: What happened to him ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: His office was abolished and he was superannuated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Yes, that was perhaps an easy way of doing it, but at all events Mr. Smith was put out of office, and the civil service list shows that Mr. Turriff occupies Mr. Smith's place, and is Land Commissioner to-day. Then there was Mr. Daniel Smith, who was a most efficient officer. He had charge of the public works in the west, and he was an active and energetic man, but he was removed from his position in the prime of life.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Surely the hou. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) does not pretend that that man was discharged without cause.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: What was the cause ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: The cause was exposed in the police court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Then the hou. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) will have an opportunity of stating it to the House. He can get up and do so if he has any charge to make. Was there any charge against Mr. Hargrave, the ex-postmaster, who is still an able and an active man ? Could there be any charge against the postmaster of Brandon, who was dismissed for partisanship, and in whose place was appointed Mr. Campbell, ex-president of the Liberal Association, and one of the most active political workers in the place. Sir, these men were removed from office by this Liberal government notwithstanding the statement of the Prime Minister and his lieutenants on the floor of this House. In view of the fact that the right lion, gentleman declared that men such as these should not be dismissed from the public service, is it not an extraordinary thing that 150 Conservative officials were dismissed from office by this government between 1896 and 1899. When the hon. member for Selkirk speaks of 400 justices of the peace being removed, let me tell him that when the Greenway government came to office the first act of their Attorney General was to pass an Order in Council cancelling all the commissions to all the justices of the peace in Manitoba, so that you could not get a Conservative justice of the peace in the whole province to make a declaration before for election purposes or any other purposes. I do not know what the Conservative party did when they came to power, but that is what the Greenway government did. If this House, to-niglit, is going to vote down the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Roche), I suppose the country will know what to expect, and for our part, we will know what conduct is to be allowed on the part of government officials in the future. I think, Sir, I have made it perfectly clear that the question that is now before the House is one which is agitating the public mind in Manitoba, and which is the cause of a great deal of public discussion in the press and on the platform. I think, Sir, it would be well for the government to tell us what action they are going to take on this matter before they call upon us to vote the salaries of some of these gentlemen. If the government say these gentlemen may take any part they wish in political affairs, so long as they do not interfere in Dominion issues, it is well for us to know that, because in a short time we shall be called upon to vote the salaries of some of them, and I do not think the minister in charge of the departments in which they are employed will find fault with us if

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: we ask the government to state distinctly what position they propose these men to occupy whether they are to be politicians in the full sense of the word, or servants of the people, who act independently of both parties. That is what we wish to know, Mr. Speaker, and before this debate is ended, I expect that we shall have the position of the government on this question clearly defined.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have ample opportunity after I have done, and I am treating him with the same amount of courtesy as the hou. member for Macdonald gave me a short time ago. There was a list of names read by the hon. member for Selkirk of respectable men, men up in years, who had given their whole lives to the service, and who were turned out practically to starve without any investigation, without any charge having been made against them, but simply because their places were required for others. There has never been, in the history of any province of this Dominion, anything like the wholesale slaughter of officials without cause as by the Manitoba government. I might allude to the case of Mr. Dawson, the very respectable police magistrate, of Winnipeg, whose place was wanted and whose head consequently dropped into the basket. Hon. gentlemen opposite are the last persons who can talk about the dismissals of officials. If there are officials in the employ of this government whom the people want to represent them in the legislature, that shows that the government have selected respectable and responsible men, who have gained high esteem in the community by the way in which they have carried out their official duties. When the Conservatives were in power there were very few of the officials whom anybody would nominate to go to parliament. I know of a case of partisanship previous to the election of 1896 in the district represented by my hon. friend from East Assiniboia, which is a case in point. An Indian agent of the late government was travelling around the country during election time, with two government horses hitched in tandem and a government official driving the team, and he was sitting back blowing a horn so as to call the farmers out and tell them how they should vote.

That was a Conservative tin-horn partisan.
There is another case to which I wish to draw my hon. friend's attention. In the election of 1887 in my district there was a gentleman who was commissioner for the purpose of settling rebellion claims. He was drawing $15 a day from the government. I could quote the figures from the public documents if any hon. gentleman wished to have them. The campaign opened in December and was kept up until the last of March. This gentleman was sent there from Ottawa, he addressed meetings, canvassed, organized, did everything he could to elect the Conservative candidate, and all the time drawing $15 a day from the treasury of the Dominion. Take another case. There was an inspector of mounted police in my district who was at the same time appointed enumerator. I went to him and wanted to see the list, and I had a perfect right to see it, being the accredited agent of one of the candidates. But he would not let me see it; he said they had no use for Grits and that I could see no list there. And, since this government came into power that officer has been promoted to be superintendent-that is his reward for treating us in that way. I could go on all night giving cases of this kind. Now, the hon. member for Marquette has claim,ed that public officials have been nominated to the legislature. I do not know anything about them. It is only rumour. I have seen the names of Mr. Young and others in the papers, but I do not know, and I fancy that no person knows, as a matter of fact whether they are officials or not. I am not going to say that it is a proper tiling for officials to take any part in elections. But I do say that the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are the last persons who should talk about partisanship of officials or the partisan dismissal of offl-pials. However, if the government looks into the case, and it is found to be in any yespect as serious as the hon. gentleman trys to make out, the government, no doubt, will see to it that these gentlemen do not continue to occupy these offices. For my part, I hold that no official has any right to go out and work in an election. But I have seen it done even last winter in Manitoba, and I venture to say if the hon. gentlemen opposite had the, opportunity again, their officials, when an election came on, would be running about the country as thick as grasshoppers. But, of course, that does not justify anything of the kind under this government, and I hope they will look into the matter. -

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
As I was not aware that this question was coming up, I shall not say more than a few words. A discussion such as we have had this afternoon can hardly be said to be of an edifying character; it seems necessarily to consist of each side charging the other
with being worse then itself. Possibly, that is inevitable under our present political system. My own opinion is that, even from the standpoint of party advantage, there is nothing to be gained by a government on coming into office discharging the employees appointed by their predecessors. But I feel equally sure that every government is in duty bound to deal with this matter purely from the standpoint of the public interest. I am pretty well acquainted with the facts in some of the cases of complaint in Manitoba that have been brought forward during the last few years. I know, as a matter of fact, there were a number of the employees of the old Greenway government who richly deserved dismissal and they got it. But it does not stop there; the very necessity of dismissing some men seem to be used as an excuse for wholesale dismissals for which there is no justification on the grounds of the public interest. One case particularly has been mentioned, that of the police magistrate for the city of AVin-nipeg. I am not in the confidence of either party there, but I can state that all parties and all fair-minded men in Winnipeg felt that the city was humiliated and that harm was done to the public service by the removal of police magistrate Dawson. A good man was removed from the public service. It matters not whether his successor was a good man or not, the fact was that a good man who was getting used to his job and able to render good public service was dismissed. I do not know what cause brought this dismissal about, but, so far as J can find out, all the public men in the pity, and the citizens generally, condemn that kind of action. Hon. geutlemen on both sides of this House have quoted full lists of officials who have been' replaced. Thie justifiable dismissals are mixed up indiscriminately with those that are purely partisan, and thus the real issue is confused. I do not regret the discussion of the matter in the House; it seems to me that it should be discussed more than it is, it should be discussed until we are sick of it, and the people of the country are sick of it, and look about for a remedy. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) read a list of dismissals. I noticed some names that had no business to be mentioned in this connection, for the parties were rightly dismissed, and dismissed for the public advantage. One case that the hon. gentleman mentioned was the dismissal of the public works officer under this government. I cannot speak from actual knowledge as to what was the alleged cause of his dismissal, but I know upon what it followed upon. I know that within a few weeks before his dismissal he grievously, and, I believe, uu-provokedly, assaulted a minor official in the customs house, a poor, weak old man- brutally assaulted him, as was proven in the police court. Of course, his dismissal ought to, and I believe did, follow as a

ft
.matter of course. It seems to me absurd that this case should be mixed up "with others in which there is legitimate cause of complaint. It must be looked upon as a scandal under the present circumstances that men who ate employees of the government, men, who, in most cases, have been appointed to the public service because they have records as active partisans-that is the outcome of the party system-should be candidates in another election while still holding public office. This seems to me to amount ,to a scandal because the public interest is sure to suffer. We cannot expect that, in the heat of an electoral contest these men, can or will deal fairly with the public whose work they are paid to do. But the cases of a lot of minor officials, men who work for the government only a part of every year or who draw small sums for minor services, should not be discussed in this connection. One case brought up by the member for Marquette was that of a subpostmaster in Winnipeg who is a candidate in the north district at the present time. 4 look upon that man as doing a public service in taking a sub-post office in his store. I believe he is serving the country in part at his own expense, as are some other officials. Still, I believe that every official .should accept the risk-if he takes a prominent part in politics or accepts nomination, and this action on his part causes irritation or trouble between them and the public whom he has undertaken to serve, the .department should immediately insist upon his withdrawing from the position in politics or handing back his commission to the government. That seems to me right and proper, purely from the standpoint of the public service irrespective of party politics. I believe it is 'a proper principle, even in party warfare, that was laid down in the declaration of the Prime Minister. It appears to me this is an opportune time to bring this question up in the House, because, as a matter of fact, preparations are only now being made for a general election in Manitoba. If the government are prepared tc tell us that the position stated in their declaration will be upheld, for my part I am prepared to accept it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
The question involved in the motion of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), it seems to me, has not been discussed, but hon. gentlemen seem disposed to discuss it from a provincial, rather than a Dominion standpoint. I remember a few years ago when reference was made to provincial civil servants in the various provinces whose governments were favourable to the present government, and when fault was found with them for taking part in politics, we were told it was a purely provincial matter, that this government had no control over matters of that kind ; therefore, it was for the provincial legislatures Mr. PUTTEE.
to deal with them. Taking that view, I think we should confine ourselves to the motion before the House. Now, I know that some members of the government entertain peculiar ideas with reference to the rights of civil servants. I may refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who, I think, is inclined to the belief that civil servants should be disfranchised. I think he stated on a former occasion that if they were disfranchised they would not get into this trouble. But I never heard any complaint from a government supporter if they did take an active part on behalf of the government. In 1887, when a Mr. McColl was a government employee in Winnipeg connected with the Interior Department, a deputation came here from Manitoba and interviewed Sir John A. Macdonald with reference to Mr. McColl's conduct in the elections. I remember the answer given to the deputation, because I was here at the time, and it was, that unless they could find some good and sufficient cause for his dismissal, Mr. McColl would not be removed from office. Sir John A. Macdonald took the ground that an employee had a perfect right to vote, and he had no fault to find with him, whether he voted Liberal or Conservative, and would not exert any influence upon him to induce him to vote Conservative. Now I find that the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Sir Louis Davies, now judge of the Supreme Court, spoke as follows in 1896 :
I say when a public official not only discharges his duty as a citizen and votes, but takes an active political part in the canvas preceding the election, and makes himself in that sense politically offensive, he takes his life in his hands, and if the party which he so actively supports is unsuccessful, his political head comes off.
I think that is quite right. I think that a civil servant who takes an active part in a political election does so at the risk of his official life, and this remark would apply whether a Liberal or Conservative government were in power. Now, I find that in 1879, when there was a change of government, the ' Globe ' of the 20tb of February, 1879, laid down this doctrine :
In the public interests there are but two considerations which can Justify the substitution of one official for another, except in cases where the holder of a place has been guilty of misconduct ; the new appointee may be better qualified for the situation than the old, or he may be able to save to the country a certain sum every year.
I think if the members of the government had carried out to the present time that principle laid down by the ' Globe ' in 1879, both sides of this House would have no reason to complain. So I say that the government should make it distinctly understood that any civil servant who takes the public platform or makes himself offensive to one party or the other, takes his official

life In his hand, and would be subject to removal from office. I find this also :
From petty officers whose remuneration is small or nominal, it is idle to expect that subserviency or decorum in regard to political matters that the government could exact in the case of highly paid officials or civil servants proper.
That was the statement made here a few years ago, and I for one think that petty officers like a great many filling positions in the Post Office Department of this country, and whose remuneration is so small, should not be deprived of any of the rights of citizens simply by reason of taking an active part in politics. I think that the Postmaster General frequently finds that it is sometimes difficult to induce a citizen to fill these paid offices on account of the small remuneration attached thereto. Therefore. I do not think that we have a right to include them in the class of persons we are discussing now. What the opposition are contending for is that civil servants who are receiving fair remuneration for their ser vices should have the right to vote if they think proper without any interference on the part of the government, but in my judgment that is as far as a civil servant should have a right to go.
Now, for the purpose of straightening out one reference that was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Selkirk, a note has been placed in my hand :
Mr. McCreary said that T. A. Cuddy, former county court clerk, Minnedosa, was dismissed and J. F. Boyd supplanted him. As a matter of fact. Cuddy was and is a Conservative, was not dismissed but voluntarily resigned, as he was removing to British Columbia. Boyd has since resigned and is now in partnership in British Columbia with Cuddy.
So you see that our hon. friends, in discussing matters of this kind, make some statements that are not in accordance with all the facts of the case, and we do not know how much credence to place on that list of dismissals that was read to us. For that reason I am not in a position to discuss intelligently the causes that have led up to the superannuations, removals, dismissals or resignations that take place in the different provinces. I think that we had better confine ourselves to looking after the civil servants of the Dominion of Canada. If the government will frankly carry out the views that they expressed in 1896, namely, that they will not encourage or allow officials to take part in politics, that is all that hon. gentlemen of this House have a right to expect of them.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL fHon. Sir William Mulock). Perhaps it is to be regretted that the discussion of a very import-' gnt principle is somewhat confounded with some individual cases. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), who introduced this motion, has rather directed it towards the application of the principle to certain
alleged violations than to the endorsement of the principle itself. After reciting in his motion the view of the right hon. Prime Minister, which represented the views of the government then and to-day, he calls, in his resolution, for censure upon the government for not having, as it is alleged, applied this principle to a particular number of cases that the hon. member gave to this House. He named a number of persons in different departments whom he says, are violating this principle. If he had communicated to the government in advance of the motion the names of the officers in question and such information as to the complaints against them as would have enabled us to make an examination, we would, upon this occasion, probably have been in a position to discuss the merits of these cases. But I think it will be conceded that you could scarcely find a more unsuitable body to determine upon questions of fact than a House such as this when the facts are not before us and are only referred to incidentally and with more or less accuracy or inaccuracy by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House. For example, the House is asked to pass a vote of censure on the government because it has not applied this principle by dismissing the gentlemen named. In support of that proposition we have the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) telling us that the government had on other occasions dismissed a larger number of officials, he stated it at 150, and he proceeded to read to the House a long list of dismissals. He read the list of, he says, 150 persons who, he says, were dismissed for violating the principle laid down by the right hon. Premier ; that is, that they were dismissed for political partisanship. The second name upon his list was that of Mr. Hargrave. I know all about the circumstances leading to his superannuation, and I have refreshed my memory since I put the question to the hon. gentleman, and it is impossible that Mr. Hargrave could have been dismissed by us for political reasons. He was a Liberal, appointed in the time of the Mackenzie government. He and his people were all Liberals, and he is a Liberal to-day. Nor was he dismissed. He was retired on a superannuation exceeding $2,000 a year. He was a highly worthy man, but Winnipeg lias suddenly grown in importance, and it was necessary to place a younger and more active man in charge of that growing office. Solely in the public interest Mr. Hargrave was retired. He himself thought that he was quite fit to carry on the business of his office and he regretted his superannuation. I retired him with regret, but I was convinced that it was necessary to do so in the public interests alone. When he was retired it was not to make a place for any one else, liecause there was no one in view, and the office was kept vacant for a considerable time until I could find a suitable person. I attached more importance to the ap-

pointment of a suitable person than to any political consideration, and in the selection we have made I think we have been successful in finding a very suitable officer to carry on that work. I dwell upon that for a moment to show how unreliable that list must be when the second name on it is one that I know does not fairly represent the class of cases to which this resolution refers. Yet we are asked to-night to dismiss all these officers without a trial and without knowing the facts. If we were to do such a thing I am sure none would be quicker to censure us than our hon. friends on the other side of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: You have done so all the time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: No, we have not done so all the time. We have reasons for our act. In regard to the general principle, we have never receded from it, but, as to its application, there must be some degree of judgment exercised. For example, when that principle was being announced by the right hon. leader of the government to parliament, it had reference immediately to Dominion oases; to officers in the Dominion service who had taken a more or less active part in Dominion politics. I am not saying that the principle is to be confined to Dominion politics, but when you come to extend it beyond the range of Dominion politics one might naturally ask how far it is to be extended. There are many sorts of contests that go on in the Dominion wherein political partisanship plays a large part, and yet these contests are not Dominion in their character. For instance, we have, as in the present instance, local politics wherein more or less Dominion issues are involved and political partisanship js awakened. We can go into another arena of conflict between the people-municipal politics. It frequently happens that party politics, in the larger sense, are introduced into municipal politics. It is not many months ago since some prominent representatives of the Conservative party in Ontario advocated municipal politics in our province being run on Dominion issues.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: So did your organizer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: We will admit for the moment, for the purpose of argument only, that a certain contest in a village turns upon Dominion politics. Is it the opinion of this House that this principle referred to shall be applied to municipal politics ? If so, there are other forms of contests wherein political questions and political partisanship will more or less play a part. I am not saying where the rule shall apply, nor would it be wise, I think, to circumscribe the rule or to define it, but it must, I think, be limited to a general and useful application. In my opinion, the first consideration on the part of any government

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: in dealing with its officers is to see that they render efficient service to the government which employs them. That is due, not only to the government, but to the people, whose servants they are, and I take the view that a public servant should be persona grata to the community, and that it is unwise for him to take part in. any conflicts in regard to the questions that divide the people into more or less hostile parties, making it unpleasant for some patrons of the office which he occupies to have to deal with such an officer. Take the example mentioned by the hon. member from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), who discussed this question temperately) and fairly, in regard to postmasters. I only illustrate the point that he sought to make in regard to postmasters enjoying a merely nominal salary. He thought that they should be allowed to enjoy all their civil rights untrammelled by any such rule as this. Let me give the illustration of a case of which I have knowledge, and we will see whether it would be safe in the public interest to tell all postmasters enjoying a merely nominal salary that they might be at liberty to engage in political struggles. I have had a complaint made to me that a certain postmaster enjoying a nominal salary-we will call it $20-a mere trifle, was an active member of a local political organization at these corners. The committee connected with the revision of the voters' lists met at the post office, and the postmaster himself was so deeply interested in the question of party politics that he intercepted a large number of the notices of appeal to the judge, with the result that one party failed to get the evidence before the judge and all the appeals were thrown out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: That was misconduct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Of course it was. But the fact that this officer took an active part in politics kept alive in him that partisan spirit, and he yielded to the temptation and misused his office, being for the moment more anxious to promote the interest of his party than to discharge his duties towards the public.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I do not think that a man who would make a capable and competent postmaster would sacrifice his citizenship for the sake of $20 a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
I am merely giving reasons why it is impossible to determine by the degree of salary or the supposed importance of the office, whether or not this rule should apply. I believe that the rule must be, that under no circumstances must a public officer be allowed to place the public interest in a secondary position. No matter how trifling the salary may be, if a man takes a public office, the country is entitled to have him give his first consideration to the public service. Another case comes to my mind where a

postmaster under a similar temptation altered the date of a number of letters containing notices for a political meeting with the result that the meeting did not take place. Therefore, you will see that no matter how trifling the position may be, it is not safe to allow a man to take part in political strife.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Did the Postmaster General make no dismissals except for offences of that kind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: X am not discussing the abstract question, and if my hon. friend desires to discuss any particular dismissal made by me I shall be pleased to discuss that with him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: The Postmaster General will have an opportunity later on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: No doubt. But, when we are discussing a question of this kind on which there is no difference between us as to the principle involved, it would be inopportune to cloud the issue by discussing particular cases. I can understand that more or less feeling is injected into this discussion, because we are told by the hon. gentlemen opposite that the question comes up at the instance of the premier of Manitoba, who reports that some Dominion officials are taking part in the expected provincial campaign. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) stated that certain Dominion officials had used their office to bring undue influence to bear upon the electors. He told us that one went to the homesteaders and brought such pressure as an officer could bring because of their being indebted to the Crown, and in another case he referred to influence being brought in connection witli timber licenses. All I have to say is that such conduct as that is highly censurable, indefensible and inexcusable, and will not be tolerated by the government. One can hardly conceive of a public officer committing a more gross interference with the liberty of the elector, than to endeavour to intimidate him by informing him of his indebtedness to the Crown, of his obligations to the Crown, and intimating to him that it may be better or worse for him according to the way he may vote. If any officers in the employ of the Dominion government are guilty of any such offence, I am sure that I can say on behalf of the government that the government will not overlook such conduct. My hon. friend has referred to two cases in my department-one of which is the case of Mr. Stratton, who he said was connected with a newspaper. I do not know what would be the proper way of treating a man who Is connected with a newspaper; whether he ought to be dismissed or whether he ought be given the opportunity of withdrawing from one or the other, or whether it would be proper under the circumstances to permit him to continue his paper. There are circumstances particular to each case which would have to be considered. You may fill a dock with accused persons but you cannot dispose of them all by the same tribunal and the same trial, unless they are jointly concerned in the same offence. Each case has to be fairly considered and tested and dealt with according to the existing law. The existing law applicable to such cases is set forth in the speech of the Premier, recited in the resolution, and that law will be properly and justly and equitably applied to all cases brought to the attention of the government. I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) on reconsideration, will deliberately ask us to-night to decide to dismiss these men. I do not know if he will persist in asking us, to here and now dismiss them or promise to dismiss them without knowing the facts. I am sure that no fair minded man would ask us to prejudge the cases, and to decide now without our knowing the facts what sort of treatment should be extended to these officers. I have only to say in conclusion, that we will deal with them in harmony with the principles laid down in 1897.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I would like to say to the Postmaster General that I brought at least two of these cases to his attention some weeks ago.

speechtext: Which two please ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Mr. Watson, postmaster and secretary of the Liberal Association

speechtext: In what way ?

speechtext: By the way of questions I put to him. X drew his attention to the fact that Mr. Jonasson was a homestead inspector and candidate, and that Mr. Watson was secretary of the Liberal Asociation, postmaster and candidate for South Brandon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I never until this moment was aware of any of these officers being involved in local politics. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche, Marquette) may have asked me some questions, but it never crossed my mind that these men were trangressiug any law. I never heard of their being identified with party politics, and I do not think the hon. gentleman will find that in any of his questions he for one moment suggested that these men were engaged in party politics.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
I do not know personally what he did, but I asked the hon. Postmaster General to bring down all the papers on which he acted, and tiiose papers contain nothing more nor less than what I have stated; because I have copies of the papers in my possession, they having been brought down in response to the motion which I made in the House for the purpose of obtaining the documentary evidence on which that man was dismissed. If there was anything further on account of which he was dismissed, all I have to say is that the hon. Postmaster General was recreant to hisi duty in not bringing it down, when 1 _ asked for all the evidence on which Air. Kaulbach had been dismissed from his position as postmaster. If the hon. gentleman knows anything more, the bon. Postmaster General did not communicate it to me, as it was his duty to do, when I moved for all the information on the subject.
Now, no one is asking the government to promise to dismiss these men. The resolution does not ask that. It simply asks the government to apply to these men in the province of Manitoba exactly the same principles that they announced in 1896, and on which they have acted so many times since. It is only in respect to the non-application of these principles that the resolution casts any censure on this government. I do not deny that mattei-s of this kind are a source

of difficulty to any government. I have no doubt whatever that they have been a source of difficulty to this government, and I have no doubt that pressure has been brought on this government to dismiss men who are still in office. But I do say that the government have yielded to pressure of that kind in a great many cases when I think it would have been better if they had held their hand or had allowed the officials the opportunity of being heard in their own defence before being dismissed. But that is not the question we are dealing with tonight. The question we are dealing with to-night is whether the government meant what they said when they laid down certain principles in this House in 1896. This resolution follows the matter up logically from beginning to end, and I will take the liberty of reading it, as it has been referred to by my hon. friend the Postmaster General. The quotations made in the resolution are only a few of many which I have under my hand, some of which have been made since the election of 1900, and in which exactly the same principles have been laid down by the right hon. leader of the government. What did my right hon. friend say in 1896 ? He said :
Now, when we find an officer in the civil service, however good a servant he may have been, however faithfully he may have discharged his duties, hut who has been an active politician, who has taken part in the election, offensively and actively, and before the eyes of the whole community, that official has become a scandal in the eyes of the community, and I have no hesitation in saying that he cannot be trusted to render faithful service to this government Where there is a government officer, he may hold his opinions, I do not care what they are ; they may be Liberal or Conservative, X do not care ; he may go and vote, and I will not inquire how he voted, but when he is seen on a public platform, when he takes part in party processions and is actively and offensively prominent as regards party candidates, that man has taken his life in his hands, and no one can have a word to say if he is dismissed from the service.
M.V right hon. friend either meant that in 1896, or he did not mean it. If it is a good principle to be applied in 1896-and it was applied in that year and the following years-it is an equally good principle to be applied now, and to be applied in the province of Manitoba as well as in other parts of Canada. Then, the first lieutenant of my right hon. friend, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, used language even more emphatic when he said :
With members of the civil service eating the bread of both parties, and deliberately interfering in elections for the purpose of aiding one political party, if they so act they must be considered as taking their political lives in their hands, and they must accept the consequences of their own acts, and the good sense of the people of the country and their natural sense of equal justice will not merely justify, but demand at the hands of the government that they should make an example of them.
The resolution after having quoted these expressions proceeds as follows :
That other members of the government, during that session and subsequent sessions, expressed the same views.
As my right hon. friend's memory of these matters may not be very good, I would like to quote some further remarks made by himself and by his colleagues bearing on the same subject. The right hon. gentleman himself, on the 1st of September, 1896, said this :
I have no hesitation in saying at this time that if anVifficer in the service chooses to he a politician, he shall be given every opportunity by this government of being a politician. What is the cause of the abominable practice which has been stigmatized in the States, that to the victor belong the spoils ? Why was it that after every Presidential election attended by a change of parties in power, the whole civil service was cleared off, the whole body of servants of the government were forced to resign or be dismissed ? The reason is obvious, the reason is that every officer under the American system was an active politician, and being an active politician it was quite natural that when the opposite party came to power the man who had been an active politician could not be a trusted servant of the government whom he had opposed.
Then, the Minister of Trade mid Commerce, dealing with the question of what is offensive partisanship, said :
There is not much difference, there may be a difference as to the definition of * offensivenes.' I should be disposed to consider, and I think I said so at the time in accordance with the principle which the hon. gentleman lays down here, that a public servant went outside of his duty and was ' offensive,' using the word in a legal sense which might properly enough apply to him, if he became a member of the committee of a candidate, or if he were canvassing actively against a candidate, I think that wculd be stepping outside the limit which has been laid down by hon. gentleman on both sides of the House.
Then he proceeds to discuss the question, whether civil servants should not be altogether disfranchised, showing that he was not referring to Dominion elections alone, but was dealing with the general question whether civil servants should interfere in political contests at all. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce again said :
It is perfectly well known, because hon. gentlemen opposite are aware that the proposition now laid down has been stated over and over by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, that where a civil servant chooses, besides exercising his undoubted right to cast his vote as he pleases, to interfere actively in elections, he must of necessity take the consequences of his own act.
And my hon. friend as late as the year 1900, when discussing the case of a certain gentleman in connection with the federal election in Gaspd. said :
Both sides of the House will agree that officers of the government should not take part in
3195 '

politics. There is something repugnant to fair-play when we see an officer of the government paid with public money, using his position amongst his friends and neighbours, where Ms connections may give him influence, for the purpose of favouring one political party.
My right lion, friend can see that there is in Manitoba the spectacle of a number of the officials of this government actively taking part in politics. Sly lion, friend the Postmaster General says that it is a provincial contest, but he admits that Domin ion issues are, to a considerable extent, involved.
