speechtext: I did not say because I did not know, but wo may presume that they are.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
I understood him to say that they were, but at all events there is no doubt that in Manitoba there is a contest going on in provincial politics between the two great parties of this country. Surely we are not to have the principle laid down that Dominion officials are to be at liberty to take an active part in provincial politics and that provincial officers are at liberty to become active partisans in Dominion politics. Every one of the cogent reasons advanced by the right hon. gentleman and the lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce applies equally to the public officers, whether they display their active partisanship in Dominion or in provincial contests, and I do not imagine that any hon. gentleman on the other side will undertake to draw a distinction of that kind. The resolution proposed by the hon. member for Marquette proceeds as follows :
The government, acting upon the principles and rules so laid down, have since dismissed a very large number of officers on the ground of alleged partisanship.
There is no question about that. Every one in this House knows that to be the case, and that it has been justified over and over in this House by hon. gentlemen opposite. Then the resolution proceeds as follows :
That an application of the principles and rules so laid own for the guidance of public officials would result in the dismissal of those officers of the government who have become ' a scandal in the eyes of the community '-
These are the right hon. gentleman's own words :

by taking an active offensive and partisan
part in the election campaign now being carried on in the province of Manitoba, and who, while * eating the bread of both parties ' ' are deliberately interfering in elections for the purpose of aiding one political party.' This House regrets that the government has not seen fit to deal with such officials in accordance with the declarations of principles so made and so often acted upon.
It seems to me that the resolution proposed by my hon. friend from Marquette is one which ought to commend itself to Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
the government. There may be something in the use of the word ' regret ' which implies a censure on the government. However, I have no doubt that my hon. friend from Marquette, if the government object to the use of that word and desii-e to affirm the principles laid down by the Prime Minister in I89G and again in 1900, would use some other word which would not be offensive to the government, in asking it to declare that these principles still prevail. If we are to have a non-partisan civil service in this country, it will not do for the government to lay down in 1890 principles such as were then laid down by my right hon. friend and to act on those from 1896 to 1903, and then in the year 1903, when the officials of this government by the dozen are in Manitoba taking an active part in the elections, calmly hold its hands and shut its eyes and say that it knows nothing about it. My hon. friend the Postmaster General suggests rather than says that the government does not know anything about those officials.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I made a very positive statement on the subject.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
The government knows about these officials just in the same way that it knew about the acts of the exMinister of Public Works. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister thought that statements published in the newspapers of speeches were sufficient to justify him in dismissing a minister of the Grown. Yet the hon. Postmaster General shuts his eyes to what is going on in the public press. He is blind to the fact that in Manitoba the names of these men are paraded from day to day in the public press or that province, on both sides of politics, and tells this House that the government have not had time to consider the question. What was denounced by the right hon. gentleman in 1896 can go on now, and the government seek to shrink responsibility by saying that they are absolutely surprised to learn that any of their officials in Manitoba are actively engaged in the political campaign going on in that province. No such pretense can save the government. The government know what is going on just as jyell as we do. They and their friends read the newspapers. These things are brought to their attention. They know every fact with regard to these men just as well as hon. gen tlemen on this side. These are facts of public notoriety. They are scandals which have been talked about in Manitoba for the last four or five weeks, and during all that time this government, which has ben so zealous since 1896 that its civil service should be free from all partisanship, will not lift its finger to suppress political partisanship on the part of civil servants, but says it knows nothing at all about it. I do not believe that any evasion of that kind will stand the government in good stead. I am bound

to assume that they meant something by the declaration they laid down in 189G. I am bound to assume that these declarations were not mere cant, and if not, the government should have taken some action before this and have made some investigation into these matters published to the world in the press for weeks past, and should compel their public officers in Manitoba, who are paid by both parties, who are eating the bread of the people of this country, to refrain from taking a partisan part in the political affairs of this country. I think that the resolution of my hon. friend from Marquette is one it was his duty to make as a representative of the province of Manitoba, and one which should commend itself to every one who believes that the government, in laying down the principles it did in 1896, was sincerely and honestly expressing its convictions and not making a mere excuse for getting rid of its political opponents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
I shall not venture to discuss the part taken by Dominion officials in the local elections of Manitoba, for that is the subject about which X know nothing. But when hon. gentlemen opposite declare that it is a horrible outrage that officials of this government should take part in the local elections on behalf of Liberal candidates, is it not as great an offence for officials of this government who are Tories to canvass and use every partisan means against the government which is now in power and which is their master ? Now, if that principle prevails in Manitoba it ought to prevail in Nova Scotia and every other province. With regard to the special incident mentioned by my hon. colleague the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) I do him the credit of saying that I do not think he knows anything personally of the circumstances. He speaks on the basis of what has been reported to him. But I think I know something personally on the subject, because X know the person and I have been present in the locality during several elections. In 1896 the Liberal Conservative party was in power. What the gentleman did during the election then I could excuse, because his patrons and friends were in power, and I do not think it is so great an offence for an official to work or use his influence for a government in power as it is for him to canvass against the government. This gentleman was petitioned against to me; the request was sent to me signed by a number of individuals that he should be dismissed. I said I could not recommend the dismissal on such grounds. The fact that an officer was a Tory, that he was opposed to the government, that he had voted against myself, was not a sufficient ground for dismissal. 1 was furnished with affidavits of three or four reputable people that this man had canvassed against the nominee of the present government, and that his house was
headquarters for the Tory party in that district. On that ground I recommended his dismissal; and I take the liberty of saying that if I discover other postmasters of this government who are guilty of the same proceedings, I will recommend the government to dismiss them also. Now, in the county of Halifax-and I think the same is general throughout Nova Scotia-the postmasters and other government officials are largely Tories. So far as I am concerned, while they do their duty they can vote Tory if they please. They ought to support the government in power, but I shall not move hand or foot against them if they exercise their franchise and do not become partisans. But if they go out of their way to canvass voters, to use their influence against this government, when the matter is brought to my notice by responsible and reputable men, I shall probably move for their dismissal. On the same principle hon. gentlemen opposite have called for the reprobation of officials that work against the government in Manitoba.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Then, you will vote for this resolution ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Oh, of course, you will vote with us too. I would like to say further that, at the time of an election, these postmasters in the county of Halifax are apt to keep literature sent out by the Liberal party for digestion at some future period, while all the Tory literature is very quickly circulated. I think a thing like that should meet with the reprehension of my hon. colleague (Mr. Borden, Halifax). No doubt his voice will be raised against it. But if I find a case of that kind and the facts are made known to me by reputable individuals supported with affidavits, I will take the liberty of moving the government to dismiss him. Every man, so far as I am concerned, shall be free to exercise his franchise according to his own ideas. But when an official of the government goes out of his way to arouse the prejudices of the people against the government and makes the post office the headquarters of the opposition party, I will move for his dismissal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend (Mr. Roche, Marquette) who has moved this resolution were really in earnest, if this object was to have the principle he affirms put in practice, he will admit, on reflection, that he has selected the very best course that could be selected to prevent the adoption of his idea. He complained that certain officers of the government in Manitoba are interfering in the elections in that province, and the first thing he does to bring the matter to the attention of the government is a motion of censure. My hon. friend shakes his head. Well, what else has been done to bring the matter to the attention of the government ? He gave his answer

a moment ago to the lion. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Muloek). He says that a few days ago he put some questions as to whether the Postmaster General had been informed of such and such matters. But if my hon. friend the Postmaster General did not take that as an intimation that the object of the hon. gentleman was to bring it to his attention that these officers were openly violating the rule laid down by the government, the hon. gentleman has only himself to blame. It is impossible to admit the doctrine laid down by the leader of the opposition on this point. He stated that the government should have known, forsooth, that there were certain officers of theirs who were candidates and taking part in the election, as was a matter of public notoriety, and their names appeared in the newspapers. But does the hon. gentleman contend that when I read the ' Telegram ' or the ' Free Press,' or any other Manitoba newspaper and see the name, for instance, of Thomas Young in the list of candidates, that I am to know that this Mr. Young is an officer of the government ? Is it to be seriously said that, looking at the newspaper and without any other information, we should know that this candidate is one of our officers upon whom we should have our eye and should see to his withdrawal from the candidature. Surely it is only reasonable to expect that, if my hon. friend on the other side has fair reason to complain that certain officers of ours are not acting up to the rules which we have laid down with regard to official conduct, it would be their business to call the attention of the government to the matter in some other way than by a motion of censure. If he had done this we should have looked into the matter. But from the statement he has made to-day I am not prepared to say I would act upon the recommendation he has made. He has selected especially three instances, those of Mr. Martin Jerome, Mr. Jonasson, and Thomas Young. As to the first instance, that of Mr. Martin Jerome, the hon. gentleman ought to know himself, in fact he cannot but know, that Mr. Jerome does not come within the category of those upon whom he wishes to invoke the censure of the government, for he is not a member of the civil service. Mr. Jerome is sometimes employed by the government, but he is not in the regular service and does not receive his cheque every month as the members of the civil service do. He has been employed from time to time by the government as a bush-ranger or in some such capacity. The hon. gentleman knows that, under such circumstances, the government has no control over Mr. Jerome and cannot call upon him to desist from being a candidate; the government has no more power over him than it would have over my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) if he were a candidate, as he will be some time. Therefore, as to this first Sir WILFRID BAURIER.
case, the hon. gentleman will find that it would have served a good purpose if, before bringing his motion in the way he has done, he had called the attention of the government to the alleged dereliction of duty on the part of Mr. Jerome.
Again, take the case of Mr. Jonasson. Mr. Jonasson, I understand, is one of our officers, I do not know in what capacity, but he is in the pay of the government. He ought not to take any part in any politics. I say deliberately that for my part I feel as strongly now, in 1SX)3, as I did in 1896, that when a man has taken a position in the civil service, he should take no part whatever in politics. He becomes an officer of the public, receiving the pay of all parties, he owes his services alone to the position which he occupies. If he wants to vote let him vote, but let him exercise his franchise in a way that will not be offensive to anybody. I say now that whenever one of our officers has been guilty of dereliction of duty, and when his name and the circumstances have been called to our attention, we shall ask him to explain whether the charge is true or not. Some time ago Mr. Robliu, the premier of the province of Manitoba, called attention to this case. I have not heard his speech, only the summary of it given to us this afternoon by the hon. member for Marquette, and he stated that it was the duty of this man either to withdraw from the political field or to withdraw from the service. Well, we cannot dismiss him unless the matter is brought to our attention. As to the case of Mr. Jonasson I understand that he has taken part in politics, as stated by the hon. member for Marquette, and in his case we shall cause inquiry to be made. But I must say that the situation is very peculiar in the province of Manitoba. There is no province in the Dominion where the political axe has been so active as in Manitoba. We have just been told that 150 dismissals have been made in Manitoba between 1896 and 1900 by this government. Sir, I challenge the accuracy of that statement, I deny it in toto. I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman from Macdonald has been misinformed. It is a long list to go through, but we have already seen three or four instances where he was shown to have been led astray, and I am satisfied that if this whole matter were investigated he would be found to be astray in one-half his cases, even more than one-half. But I do not admit a single case where we have been derelict, either in Manitoba or elsewhere, I do not admit there has been a single dismissal except for cause. But in the province of Manitoba, unfortunately, there have been dismissals by wholesale. At this very moment when my hon. friend from Marquette, in a moment of exasperated virtue, asks us to call upon our officers to withdraw, to stay their hand- at this very moment I have information that officials of the local government are openly

taking part in elections. It may not be true, I hope it is not true; but I am inclined to believe there is some truth in it, according to a speech which we had this afternoon by the member from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). He gave the whole case away when he stated of his own party : We have made no pledges in that matter, we have no policy and no principle in that matter.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I did not say that, that we had no principle in the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I must be candid with my hon. friend, I am glad to hear that he repudiates the doctrine. But though he did not say that in so many words, he did say this : We have made no declaration on this point, but the government have made a declaration on this matter and they must be compelled to live up to it. Then by implication, if the Conservative party have made no declaration, therefore they are at liberty to do as they please. If my hon. friend does not admit that kind of logic, at least it is applicable to the case. But I am glad to accept his disclaimer, not only in words but in spirit also, that they have no principle in the matter. I believe that he wants us in the province of Manitoba to live up to our doctrine, and we shall take good care that his own side also shall live up to that doctrine, which seems to meet with his approval. I have only to say with regard to this motion that 'it is a vote of censure where no censure whatever has been incurred. With regard to the information which the hon. gentleman says he gave to the Postmaster General, my hon. friend has just given me the question which the hon. member for Marquette asked the minister a few days ago :

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
1.	Is Mr. S. Jonasson an employee of the De-partmeiit of the Interior, in the province of Manitoba, as forest-ranger or homestead inspector ?
2.	If so, is the government aware that he is the Liberal candidate for the constituency of Gimli in the ensuing provincial elections ?
3.	Will his services be continued by this government while he is engaged in party politics.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.

1.	Yes.
2.	The government has no information that Mr. Jonasson is a candidate for Gimli.
3.	If he is a candidate, he will not be continued as a salaried official of the department.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock) :

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
The Postmaster General seeks to obscure the evidence of dismissals that have taken place from time to time in various parts of Canada. These chickens will come home to roost, Mr. Speaker, and no doubt the hon. gentlemen will live to regret many times the action they have taken in many individual instances during the years they have been in power. When the statement is made that every dismissal of postmasters and others has been made for good cause, Sir, 101
I take exception to that statement in so far as our district at least is concerned. I am not going to speak for the province of Manitoba, but for the section of country from which I come. There have been dismissals made without cause, without the slightest cause, and which do not redound to the credit of the Postmaster General or of this government. The Postmaster General is perfectly aware of the fact. I brought it to his attention at the time, that when Miss Angus was dismissed no cause whatever was alleged. That young lady kept a country post office, on her salarv depended her own livelihood and that of her mother; and the government committed a cruelty in dismissing her which shall never be forgotten in that section of the country, or in this House, so long as I am here as the representative of that constituency. I am perfectly willing that this government or any other should enjoy the legitimate fruits of power. I do not object to that, I expect them to do it. I expect them to reward their friends. I do not object to that so long as they do not interfere with the public interest. But when they do, of course they must expect to be subjected to the criticism to which they are entitled. But, Sir, when they go out of their way to serve miserable, low, sectional, party interests, in some small communities that should be beneath the consideration of any department or any minister, when they descend to that depth, they must expect to be criticised and blamed for it. I would call the attention of the right hon. leader of the government to the fact that he only read one of the answers to those questions. It is peculiar that even in this House, where books are open and where more than one man can read, we should find the right hon. leader of the government forgetting himself and the high dignity of his position to such an extent as a partisan that he has failed in his effort to be fair. We find him reading one question put by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), the answer to which gave an opportunity of applause from the hon. gentlemen who sit behind him. The answer to that question was :
If he is a candidate, he will not be continued as a salaried official of the department.
Applause from hon. gentlemen behind. But, the other question is this :
1.	Is the government aware that Mr. John Watson, postmaster at Nesbitt, Manitoba, is the president of the South Brandon Liberal Association ; and the Libera] candidate for that constituency in the ensuing elections in that province ?
2.	Will his services be continued by this government while he is engaged in party politics?
. The POSTMASTER GENERAL CHon. Sir William Mulock). The department has no information whatever as to whether Mr. John Watson is the president of the South Brandon Liberal Association or the Liberal candidate for that constituency in the ensuing elections in that province.



That does not say what is going to happen to him. If the right hon. gentleman had read that one would he have received that applause ? I do not believe he would have received it. I would like to know from the hon. Postmaster General how much correspondence he has in regard to this man being a candidate. This was on the 8th of April, and it is now the 15th of May. It takes three or four days to communicate with that part of the country and the hon. Postmaster General has had five weeks in which to ascertain the facts. I would like to see the correspondence brought down and placed on the Table showing how much interest the hon. minister had taken in that question during the past five weeks. I will venture to say that he has taken none whatever. I am sure the hon. gentleman has never thought of it and never intended to think of it again if this debate had not been 'brought up. Now, the right hon. leader of the government says :	You are
in great haste. You should have prepared your resolution in other terms if you wished to win the object you seem to seek. There was a question asked in regard to Mr. Jerome in 1899, by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) and what was the answer to it ? The right hon. gentleman says:	We pay him spasmodically. We
pay him when it suits our purpose. When we can have some excuse for rewarding this political tool we pay, but when it is inconvenient, when there is an election on hand, when we want to have our hands clean so that we can hold them up to high heaven and say :	Look at the grand principles that were laid down by this government two or three years ago. When we want to stand in that sort of atmosphere we do not pay Mr. Jerome. We pass over thirty or sixty days and then we give him his back-pay because that gentleman receives, as bush-ranger, or forest-ranger, the pay which is good enough for any man. He is receiving a great deal more to-day than he would as a legislator of the country and he is under a far greater obligation to the political organization that creates this government than he is to his legislative duties so far as measuring it by dollars and cents is concerned. The hon. Postmaster General claimed great credit for the easy way in which he has disposed of the venerable ex-postmaster of Winnipeg. He seemed to think that he had got rid of that gentleman in most beautiful style, in a way that should have felt comfortable to the poor old man. He removed him because he was getting old. He was as strong and vigorous as he is to-day. Every man who goes to Winnipeg and sees him knows that he is one of the examples that is pointed out, and as we go there we are reminded of the great fight that took place for a whole year between Mr. McIntyre and Mr. Conklin as to who should get the position vacated by the postmaster. That was the question

speechtext:
at issue. They would have dismissed the postmaster a year before they did if they could have arranged for his successor. That gentleman enjoyed his salary for a year longer than was intended. lie would have been officially executed by the lion. Postmaster General twelve months previously and he would have been relieved of the pain and trouble that worried him so much. They worried him so that he remained in office for over seventeen years and is still alive and in good health, I wish the hon. Postmaster General would prescribe some such worry for me. In 1899 the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) asked :
1.	Is Mr. Martin Jerome an employee of the Interior Department in the province of Manitoba as forest-ranger or in any other capacity ?
2.	If so. is he the same gentleman who is the Liberal candidate for the constituency of Carillon in the ensuing elections in that province?
3.	Will his services be continued by the government while he is engaged in party politics ?
This is the answer :

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
1. Mr. Martin Jerome is an employee of the Interior in the province of Manitoba as forest-ranger. 2. Inquiry has elicited the fact that Mr. Jerome has been tendered but has not accepted a nomination for the legislature.
3.	Should Mr. Jerome accept the nomination his employment in.his present capacity will cease.
That was' in 1899. Do you not see how they got out of that 1 It does not say anything about his being elected. If he were elected then he would become intensely useful to hon. gentlemen opposite, and they could not afford to get rid of him. Mr. Jerome was the gentleman wh6 commanded the situation in this case-not the government. The government were bound to keep Mr. Jerome. If he had been defeated and driven from politics they possibly could have afforded to sacrifice him as they did that poor old gentleman who represented the splendid Liberal principles of Alexander Mackenzie's time, but who had to make way for Mr. McIntyre who wanted that office. I shall be pleased to read a letter to the right hon. gentleman which will interest him and I am sure it is one in which he will have some faith. It is addressed to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd), and it reads as follows :
Premier's Office,
Winnipeg, May 4, 1903.
N. Boyd, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
My dear Boyd,-I have your letter of the 30th April and have noted its contents. Am pleased to see that the party purposes to compel the government to make a declaration as to the propriety of homestead inspectors, particularly in the country canvassing and using their positions as officials of the Dominion government to intimidate electors into voting against convictions and further charging up their expenses in connection with canvassing and organization meetings, as an expense in discharge of official duties. It certainly is the greatest outrage that has ever been perpetrated in this country and

I cannot believe that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who so far as I know him, is an honourable' man, will permit this sort of thing to continue. There is no question about the facts, they are absolutely indisputable and therefore you and others can make as strong statements as you like, as to what they are doing. Only on Saturday an Icelander came in 40 miles to report to me a meeting that he attended when out north of St. Laurent at which Captain Jonasson was present and spoke, but would not allow a single representive of the government a moment of time in which to address the meeting and the burden of his cry was his ability to do them favours as homestead inspector. These are the reports that come to me by men that feel the effects of his presence. I have not yet seen Powers or Barrett, but I presume will in the course of a few days.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) R. P. ROBLIN.
Those are facts. Those facts can be ascertained by this government. Why, to say that this government know nothing of what is going on in Manitoba, to say that they have no interest in the election in Manitoba, when the hon. Postmaster General can stand up in this House and say that he is one of the members of the Liberal government that has no knowledge of what is going on in Manitoba, that he does not read the public press the same as other people in this country, is something that it is hard for hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to accept. Why, Mr. Speaker, he reads it here half the time in our faces when we are talking to him. I believe the Postmaster General to be a great reader of newspapers. I have seen him spend hours reading them In this House when we wanted his attention. Surely he must read something besides the Toronto ' Globe ' and the Toronto ' Star.' X feel positive that the Postmaster General made a mistake, and that if he ever gets an opportunity he will never make that speech of his over again in just the same way. He is a reading man. He knows that there is an election pending in Manitoba; he knows from the questions which were put to him by the hon. member for Marquette, and which he answered, that these gentlemen are candidates and employees of this government. He knows it from the letter which I have read to-night from the hon. Mr. Roblin. He knows that his friends behind him have made no defence to-night. True, they have said that we did the same thing, but two wrongs do not make a right, and that is no argument. He knows that his own supporters do not get up to defend him to-night, and he knows that they know that there is an election in Manitoba and that these men are candidates in that election. The minister must be franker with this House. Perhaps it is that they are sorry for the principle they have laid down. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that every time the Postmaster General attempts to tie himself up to high minded principle he is sorry for it, and the same thing ap-101$
plies to the Prime Minister, and to the other members of the cabinet. During their whole political life they have been trampling under their feet every principle that they had, whether in power or out of power. Sir, there is a sacred principle involved in this resolution, a principle set forth in the very words of the Prime Minister, and we ask him to enforce that principle, and to vindicate his words. X ask him for the sake of himself, for the sake of his government, and for the sake of the country to enforce that principle without hesitation, and not go back on his words again. If there is a word in that resolution that he would like to have struck out let him ask the hon. member (Mr. Roche) to strike it out, and my hon. friend will do so. But, above all, let the Prime Minister enforce his declared principle which is recorded in his own words in the pages of ' Hansard.' Let the right hon. gentleman enforce this principle, I say it again, and let him declare to the people of this country that the first duty of himself and his government is to represent the people of Canada, whether they be Liberals or Conservatives, or Grits or Tories.

speechtext: I suppose this is a case of a gentleman having what is called a soft job. I notice that in 1901 there was a vote of $6,000 taken for that work; in 1902. $3,000, and now in 1903-4, $5,000 is being asked. These are the amounts in the main estimates, probably if I examined the supplementary estimates I should find other votes as well. Certainly the government ought to be able to show that there is very important traffic on that river. The keeping up of an expenditure of this kind year after year becomes a very serious question. Here we find an average of about $5,000 a year spent for three years. There should be very important traffic to warrant such important expenditure. My hon. friend from Macdonald (Sir. Boyd) has pointed out that in the province of Slanitoba. there are very pressing works there for which it does not seem possible to get a dollar, and I know of many urgent cases in Ontario. I am not trying now to raise any sectional issue. But, wherever such work is located, where so much is spent there ought to be urgent public reasons for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) might go back to 1883, 1884, and 1S85, if this is an undeserving work. Tlie hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is an old member of the House, and he might go back ten or fifteen years, during which nearly the same amount of money was spent from time to time on this work. Of course, that is no justification, if the work is not a proper one, but I have heard no intimation that it is not. The chief engineer informs me that the reason we are asking this amount this year is that there

is a rocky skoal to be removed, which will lessen the future expenditure necessary. If that is correct, I hope the hon. gentleman will see that it is better to spend a little money and try to do the work properly than go on as we have been doing for the last twenty years, spending money and not doing any good. The chief engineer tells me that if this money is spent, the same expenditure which has gone on, the amounts which have previously been expended will not be required in the future.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Perhaps the engineer will explain what was done with this $6,000 in 1901, when there is still this rock to be removed and $5,000 is being asked tills year ? I do not know whether that money was spent, but the vote was asked. Was it to remove part of this rock, or has the engineer discovered all of a sudden that there is this rock requiring an expenditure of $5,000 for its removal ? My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) is too good a business man. and too logical, when he thinks proper to be logical, to use as a justification for useless expenditures now, the statement that there were useless expenditures under the former government. I do not think we can afford to carry the mistakes of either the Liberal or the Conservative governments. We must judge our expenditures by the advantage they yield to the public. I hope the hon. gentleman will not lay down any contrary principle. Speaking for myself, I am not here to defend a single act, either deliberate or mistaken, with regard to previous expenditures in this country. It is our plain duty to see to it that the public money is expended only upon works necessary in the public interest. Now, if there is any traffic in this river, it would seem to be of a feeble character, for the hon. gentleman has not told us what it is as a justification of this expenditure. Even though the traffic is small, if this expenditure completed the work, it would be a different matter. But, if we are to go on with large expenditures year after year for no better reason than that advanced by the hon. gentleman, I venture the opinion that we have no real reason for the voting of this money at all. We have come to the time in Canada, when, so far as taking the public money for merely political purposes is concerned, we can afford to retrace our steps. If the former government has been guilty of expenditures of that kind, that is no reason why the Liberal party should pursue the same course, or why, pursuing it, they should cite the actions of their predecessors as justification for what they are doing. Our expenditures are becoming more pressing; new districts are opening up and demands are becoming greater than our revenues will meet. We have come to the time when both parties can afford to learn by the mistakes of the past. I am not making charges, but, I fear that neither side can hold themselves guiltless in this respect. I know there is always some difficulty in a government resisting pressure from the outside. I know that there are many cases that are meritorious probably while there are others in regard to which extreme pressure is brought to bear for the purpose of having an expenditure made that governments have to yield to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I said most emphatically that it was no justification for asking a vote to say that it was an improper expenditure in the past. I did not use that as an ai'gument why the amount should be voted, but, the other night, when the subject was under discussion, I was asked by an hon. gentleman opposite how long this dredging had been done on this river, and in answering the question, I said I did not think it should be considered an improper work. I said that parliament had voted an appropriation for such a long time that it must be a justifiable work, not as the hon. member for Both-well states, for improper or for political purposes. I may mention that the constituency was a Liberal constituency while the late Conservative government made this expenditure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Circumstances may have changed very materially.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) will say that this amount was spent for the purpose of influencing this constituency. The only argument I used was that this work, having been carried on, it was fair to assume that it was a necessary work. There has been no statement made in this House or out of it to indicate that there has been anything improper about it. I was acting on the advice of the chief engineer of the department in regard to it. I dare say that the former ministers must have asked for an appropriation for this work because they thought it was a desirable work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
I think the hon. Minister of Public Works will readily conceive that circumstances may have changed. I am not talking about the political complexion of the constituency, because, in discussing these questions, we should take a broader view than that altogether. We can readily believe that in years gone by, that river was a more important means of communication for the people and their produce than it is to-day, from the fact that they may not have had railway facilities in the years gone by. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am sure that you will agree with me that the traffic cannot be very great on a river that only serves seven or eight miles of territory. We are spending $5,000 a year. I will venture, with assurance, to say that $5,000 will carry all the commodities raised on twelve miles of river to market by railway, and I understand there is a railway crossing that river and running to Montreal. This question should be looked into. I do

not know but that there was timber floating down that river in former years, for which it was important to have this dredging done. 1 want to say to the hon. gentleman that it was his business to have criticised the expenditures of the former administration, not ours. I venture the assertion that these expenditures were pretty severely criticised, because former governments were more severely criticised for their expenditures than the hon. gentleman and his department are by the present opposition to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: That is the reason I assume the expenditure must have been all right, because, I suppose, it would have been criticised before if St had not been considered a proper expenditure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I may say that twelve or fourteen years ago there were two steamers, the * Filgate ' and ' Cliateau-guay ' plying between Beauharuois, Chat-eauguay, Lachiue and Montreal. Since the building of the New York Central Railway there is a certain amount of traffic which finds its way to the railway station and goes by railway. Now, there is only one boat plying between Beauharnois, Chateauguay, Lachine and Montreal daily, carrying farmers' produce from Chateauguay and Lachine to Montreal. I may also say that the excursionists who come out to Lake St. Louis find it much more convenient to take the boat in the morning than to wait for the New York Central train which arrives at Montreal at 9.45 a.m. The boat often finds itself unable to take all the trade that is offered, and in fact it would almost pay to put another boat on the route.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Who owns the boat ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: It is owned by a company. I cannot tell you who are the owners. It is called the ' Chateauguay.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Can you tell us the tonnage of the boat ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I cannot tell you that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Can you tell us the draft of the boat, or anything about it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: That information has already been given.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: It draws six feet of water, I am told. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brown) has told us that this steamboat is used for the purposes of certain citizens of Montreal in going up and down the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: No, that was not the statement I made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: No, but that was the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brown).

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Nor did my hon. friend (Mr. Brown) say so. He said that it was used by excursionists.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Chateauguay make himself plain on that point ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: The steamboat ' Chateauguay ' takes people from Chateauguay and St. Philippe. There is a large amount of produce shipped from these points. The New York Central will not place cars on their train to accommodate the people there, and they send their produce by this boat in the early morning. It is for the accommodation of the farmers, and the boat can hardly carry all the produce which is offered to it in the morning. Sometimes five or six loads of hay and 300 barrels of apples have to remain on the wharf for two or three days.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: What class of produce is being sent from there now that so completely overtaxes the capacity of the boat V

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Hay, at this season of the year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I may say that there are not only boats carrying passengers from these points. There are tow boats taking barges. There is a very great amount of hay shipped to Montreal from that locality. There are fruits, and there is a great amount of other trade taken from points which are not served by the railways. I am not so familiar with the locality as the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Brown), but I know for a fact that tug boats are going there, getting barges and taking them to Montreal loaded with grain and hay. The people of these parishes who are not served by the railways are obliged to bring their hay and load it on these barges. There is a large amount of freight coming out of this twelve miles of territory, not six miles, as some hon. gentleman has stated. There are twelve miles of that river that must be dredged, and if it is not dredged, we will have to close up the river, which would preclude the people of several parishes from sending their freight to the city of Montreal, for instance, fruit. Without a railroad these people could not ship their fruit. I think this is absolutely necessary. I suppose it must have been taken into consideration by the late government, and rightly so. That work must be done every year, or else the river must be closed to navigation, to the great detriment of these people.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman has just said. But I want to repeat what I have always said in this House that the government are neglecting some other places. There is the New York Central Railway running from Montreal through that and other localities, and there is the other road called the Adirondacks, which goes up into that country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: It is the same road.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
Well, if you don't know I do. Of course it is very handy to

have a railroad built through every parish, by every church door and to every farmer's house, I admit that. But why is it that in the county of Dorchester the government has never given one cent to build a railroad, the only road we have there is the Quebec Central. People have subscribed and given money and labour to build a road. I must tell you this much, that we have from fifty to seventy-five miles to go to the city of Quebec and we have to haul our stuff with horses. We have been asking ever since I have been in this parliament- nearly seven years-for help from this government to build not in the county of Dorchester, but in the county of Beauce, nine miles of road. This nine miles of road would serve over 19,000 people in the counties of Beauce, Dorchester and Bellechasse. Yet I have failed to obtain one cent of help from the government to accommodate the people of these three counties. The people of Bellechasse have to haul forty miles, the people of Beauce have to haul thirty or forty miles, and the people of Dorchester, thirty or thirty-five miles in order to get to a railroad. We have never asked the government for any help except to build that nine miles of road. There is not a bridge to be built on the route, it is an easy route to build upon, yet we are refused assistance. I have worked for this road ever since I came to this House. I have tried to get both members from the county of Beauce to work for it. I do not know whether they have or not, but they tell me they have. I say plainly to this House it is a shame for the government to treat one county better than another. We all help to support this government with our money, and we should be treated alike, if not alike, then as nearly so as possible. Now, I would like any one, young or old, rich or poor, to show me where or when this government has ever paid one cent or one dollar towards helping the people in the county of Dorchester. We built a court house, the county built it. A few years ago I asked the ex-Minister of Public Works to give us $200 for a county bridge; not one cent did I get.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Was it the Minister of Public Works for the Dominion or for the local House that you asked for assistance ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Mr. Israel Tarte, the hon. member for Montreal, was the gentleman.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: For a court-house in your county ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
No, for a bridge. I see there is an ice pier to be built at Richmond, well we will see about that soon. We have rivers running through my county as big as the St. Francis river at Richmond, logs are floated on that river, on both rivers. Neither one of them is navigable. Here is an item for a pier, but when I ask for $200 to build a
county bridge, after four bridges had been washed away and the people got tired of building, I was refused. I suppose if I had been a Liberal I might have got it; but I was not, and I will not be.
Harbours and rivers, Quebec, chargeable to capital.-River St. Lawrence ship canal, $515,800.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I think, in view of the lateness of the hour, and that some representatives from Quebec who wished to discuss this item are absent, we had better adjourn.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Perhaps the proper thing to do would be to accede to the request of the hon. gentleman. At the same time, I think some little consideration should be shown to the minister. This is the fifth or sixth time this vote has been called and asked to stand on account of the absence of one or two members. While I would be willing always to wait for an absent member, I think there ought to be some reasonable consideration shown to the public business. I ask my hon. friend if it is not right, after the item has been postponed several times at the request of hon. gentlemen opposite, that at last we should get down to business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I am bound to agree with the Iron, the minister to this extent, that I think perhaps there is too much of a habit on both sides of the House to spend only a small portion of Friday in Ottawa. The result of that habit, which is not peculiar to either one side or the other, and which has been in force for many years, is that we practically have only about three days in the week to do our work. I for one would be very glad if some change would be made in that respect, so that we should have five days to do the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: I want to point out to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, that the delay in getting through with his estimates has been the result of matters requiring to be brought to the attention of the House with the perfectly fair object of having them discussed. For example, the day before yesterday we discussed the Treadgold concession, and although we may differ in opinion about it, no one will say that it was not a proper matter to be discussed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
To-day we have been discussing an important matter brought before us by my hon. friend from Marquette. Yesterday the minister would have got into supply and probably substantial progress would have been made, were it not for a cause which was not in any way due to members on this side of tile House, and on account of which the time was taken up with matters which were not very, profit-

able to tbe country or to any of us. While I agree that there is some force in the hon. minister's remarks, still I want him to remember the circumstances which I have brought to his notice. It is a fair proposition that some day should be fixed for the discussion of these items, and that the House would be so notified. If he will communicate to me now, or at any later time, his views with regard to that, he will find us disposed to give him an opportunity to have the items discussed in the committee, and discussed in such a way that he will not be brought here from day to day; although as a matter of fact, I suppose we are entitled to his presence in the House during a considerable portion of the time. In any case, it is always a great pleasure to have the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) here.
The MINISTER OF PUBT/IC WORKS. I agree that it is my duty to be here all the time, and I am perfectly willing to discharge that duty. I think, however, that these gentlemen who asked for three or four adjournments should remain here as well as the rest of us. No doubt there ought to be given a reasonable time to discuss the estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who kept us all day yesterday discussing the teapot, has not been in the House tonight.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext: It Was the absence of one or two members who asked items to stand, that I spoke of. That is hardly fair to the rest of us. They are absent on their own pleasure or business and they should not prevent ns from carrying on the business of the House. If I ask the House to sit a little late some night when these gentlemen are present, I hope no objection will be taken.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTERFERENCE OF CIVIL SERVANTS IN ELECTIONS.
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, House adjourned at 11.30 a.m.

Monday, May 18, 1903.
